items.content: NeurIPS 2026 The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems Sydney (Main) Dec 6 - 12 Pricing Registration Atlanta (Satellite) Dec 9 - 13 Pricing Registration Paris (Satellite) Dec 9 - 13 Pricing Registration View Hotel Information Quick Links Helpful resources Invited Speakers Latest Announcements Stay updated with conference news All Sydney & Atlanta waitlists were activated on Oct. 27 at 10 am PDT. More registrations will be released on Oct. 30 10am PDT. Authors with unused reserved registration spots are reminded to register urgently. Paper locations have been assigned, authors can now register: Author Registration Information Paper presentation preferences emails to Authors have been sent, responses are due by Sept. 30 AOE The Career site is open See this blog post for details on the registration process Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. items.content: NVIDIA and Oracle Expand NVIDIA Vera Rubin to Multi-Gigawatt Scale and Bring NVIDIA Vera CPU to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and NVIDIA Vera CPUs Are Now Generally Available on OCI, With Plans to Introduce HGX Rubin NVL8 Systems to Help Organizations Accelerate Frontier Model Training, Improve Inference Efficiency and Scale Agentic Workloads October 27, 2026 NVIDIA and Oracle today announced plans to expand Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Superclusters with NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems to multi-gigawatt scale, supporting growing customer demand for AI training, inference and agentic applications. Oracle and NVIDIA also expanded their AI infrastructure collaboration with the general availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI. The expanded collaboration gives customers infrastructure for both the GPU-intensive work of training and serving frontier models and the CPU-intensive tasks agents perform between model calls, including executing tools, testing code and retrieving data. Customers can scale CPU and GPU resources independently to match their workloads, helping reduce idle capacity and put more of their infrastructure to productive use. OCI Superclusters Help Organizations Bring Frontier AI to Market Faster at Multi-Gigawatt Scale OCI Superclusters combine NVIDIA NVL72 rack-scale systems, Oracle Acceleron networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X ™ Ethernet networking featuring NVIDIA Spectrum™-6 switches and NVIDIA BlueField®-4 DPUs, and gigawatt-class power and cooling to train and serve the largest AI models. Each rack connects 72 GPUs through NVIDIA NVLink ™ scale-up networking, while OCI’s resilient, multiplanar network scales across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. The planned Vera Rubin expansion builds on OCI’s existing NVIDIA-powered infrastructure, including NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems. NVIDIA’s common CUDA® software foundation and continued software optimization help customers support evolving models and workloads across hardware generations. OCI also plans to introduce NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8, delivering eight Rubin GPUs connected through NVLink in an x86-based server configuration. The planned platform features two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 CPUs, 4TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps of high-speed RDMA networking, providing a flexible deployment option for AI training, fine-tuning and inference. HGX Rubin NVL8 enables customers to adopt next-generation Rubin GPU technology in a smaller eight-GPU configuration while maintaining compatibility with x86-based applications. This flexibility enables customers to adapt their AI infrastructure to different models and workloads as their needs evolve, using accelerated computing capacity across both training and inference to make better use of their infrastructure investments. OpenAI has demonstrated how this infrastructure supports frontier AI. In Abilene, OpenAI has trained and served GPT-6 Astra on an OCI Supercluster with more than 100,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs . “As our frontier models advance, we need infrastructure that can keep pace,” said Sreekanth Pothanis, engineering leader, compute infra at OpenAI. “NVIDIA Vera Rubin on OCI gives us the computing performance and scale to accelerate model training and serve increasingly demanding AI workloads.” NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI Accelerate the Work Behind AI Agents AI agents do more than generate responses. They call tools, execute code and retrieve information to complete tasks. Slow execution of those CPU-intensive operations can delay results and leave GPUs waiting between model calls. OCI Compute with NVIDIA Vera CPUs combines high single-thread performance with memory bandwidth to help agents complete CPU-intensive tasks faster. High single-thread performance accelerates individual tool calls and code execution, while high memory bandwidth keeps CPU cores supplied with data as agents run concurrent tasks. Together, these capabilities help reduce GPU idle time and maintain consistent performance as workloads scale. To further support these workloads, OCI Kubernetes Engine enables customers to scale CPU and GPU resources independently, while Oracle Acceleron provides hardware-based isolation for workloads running untrusted, AI-generated code. Customers with early access to NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI, including OpenAI, are exploring their potential across a range of AI workloads. “NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI deliver the world-class loaded performance needed to execute code and run tools across our rapidly growing agentic sandbox workloads,” said Uday Ruddarraju, chief technology officer of compute at OpenAI. “We are bringing Vera into production on OCI to support these workloads at scale.” “Oracle Cloud Infrastructure gives customers the performance, security and scale to advance frontier AI,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Oracle. “Our collaboration with NVIDIA extends those capabilities across training, inference and agentic AI. By combining NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs with Oracle Acceleron networking and AI-optimized data centers, we’re helping customers keep GPUs productive, secure and scale efficiently as their needs grow.” “AI factories must be productive, durable and fungible — delivering efficient computing, remaining useful through continued software advances and serving different models and workloads as demand changes,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “With Oracle, we’re bringing Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs to OCI to help customers put more of their infrastructure to work today and sustain its value as AI evolves.” Learn more about Oracle Acceleron , Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Supercluster , Oracle and NVIDIA’s multigenerational partnership , and OCI Compute with NVIDIA Vera CPUs . items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.content: Data Center / Cloud Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4 Using the open-source GPU Fractioning Operator and KAI Scheduler to enforce per-workload memory limits at scale Oct 27, 2026 By Ekin Karabulut , David Lifshitz and Hagay Sharon Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary GPU Fractioning Operator is a new open-source Kubernetes operator hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub. It runs alongside the NVIDIA GPU Operator to set up and supervise Multi-Process Service (MPS) on every GPU node, apply per-workload memory limits and compute modes, and measure memory and compute use per GPU fraction rather than per whole GPU. CUDA 13.4 introduces a memory boundary enforcement that is transparent to applications, offering exact memory amounts, guaranteed minimums with burstable maximums, and a choice between time-slicing and sm-sharing compute modes. KAI Scheduler v0.18.0 integrates with GPU Fractioning through its NvFractions GPU-sharing mode, writing per-container Pod annotations that specify memory requests, limits, compute mode, and GPU device assignments for the operator to enforce on the node. Administrators can enable NvFractions during KAI Scheduler installation with a Helm flag, and workloads declare fractional GPU requirements using annotations such as absolute memory sizes, portion-based fractions, optional burst limits, and compute mode selection. Next Steps Explore the GPU Fractioning Operator repository for installation and configuration instructions. Review the admin guide and user guide for the three GPU sharing mechanisms. Join the Slack channel or bi-weekly community meetings to ask questions and contribute. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU. Giving each one an entire device can leave capacity idle; sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the infrastructure they already have. NVIDIA GPUs already support several approaches to sharing. Multi-instance GPU (MIG) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances that are transparent to the application, time-slicing lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces (sm-sharing). CUDA 13.4 now enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application with a new time-sharing mode, alongside the compute sharing mode (sm-sharing) that already existed in MPS. Here is what the CUDA release brings: An exact memory amount: A workload asks for a memory size and CUDA holds it there. An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU. A range: A workload gets a guaranteed minimum plus a maximum it can grow into when memory is free. A compute mode: Each workload can choose to use its compute in an sm-sharing mode rather than using the default time-sharing mode. A transparent memory limit: Each workload sees only a fraction of the GPU memory. The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes CUDA provides the memory enforcement capability, but a Kubernetes cluster can’t use it on its own. On every GPU node, something has to: Run and supervise the daemons that these features depend on Apply each Pod container’s memory limits and compute mode before the process starts Report what each fraction actually uses, rather than what the whole GPU uses This work belongs on the node, independent of whichever scheduler placed the workload. GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator A new open-source Kubernetes operator, gpu-fractioning , is hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub. It runs next to the NVIDIA GPU Operator, which provides the driver and the container runtime setup. GPU Fractioning Operator handles three jobs: It sets up and runs MPS on every GPU node. It applies each workload’s memory limits and compute mode. It measures memory and compute use per fraction rather than per GPU. How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator The developers write the resource and mode annotations in the pod YAML. Then the scheduler selects the GPUs for a workload and records its memory allocation and compute-sharing mode in per-container Pod annotations. GPU Fractioning Operator reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to apply the workload’s memory limits and compute mode: Annotation Meaning nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.request Guaranteed GPU memory nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.limit Maximum the container may grow into nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpus.devices Which GPUs the container was assigned Table 1: Per-container Pod annotations that GPU Fractioning Operator reads to enforce a GPU fraction Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA. The scheduler still has its own job: choosing a GPU with enough free memory and never mixing compute modes on one GPU. Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler KAI Scheduler is the first scheduler integrated with gpu-fractioning . Starting with v0.18.0, KAI Scheduler has a GPU-sharing mode called NvFractions . KAI Scheduler picks which slice of which GPU each workload gets and writes the annotations (see Table 1, above), and gpu-fractioning enforces them on the node. KAI Scheduler’s other sharing modes stay available, and administrators choose one per cluster. It can be enabled when KAI is installed: helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \ -n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \ --set global.nvFractions.set=true This also installs gpu-fractioning as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations. There are four important annotations that answer four questions: 1. How much memory is needed 2. How far the workload may grow 3. How compute is shared 4. How many GPUs it spans How much memory: The request There are two ways to request memory: 1. As an absolute size: Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units: The container name ( app ) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container. 2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation: gpu-fraction: "0.5" How far it may grow: The limit This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request: Request Type Annotation Example Absolute Size nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit “80Gi” A Portion kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit “0.8” Table 2 : Which limit annotation to use for each type of memory request The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the gpu-fraction and less than 1. How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing Figure 1. Time-slicing divides the GPU’s time. SM-sharing divides its streaming multiprocessors (sm) Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together. Time-slicing is serial: Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation. SM-sharing is parallel: The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain. Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container: nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # or "time-slicing" A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs. How many GPUs are utilized To get fractional capacity on several devices, add: gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4" The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs. Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: inference labels: kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue annotations: nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi" nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi" # optional nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4" # optional, default 1 spec: schedulerName: kai-scheduler containers: - name: app image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04 This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together. Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default): metadata: annotations: gpu-fraction: "0.5" gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8" # optional nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "time-slicing" # optional gpu-fraction-num-devices: "2" # optional spec: schedulerName: kai-scheduler containers: - name: app This is an example for a development or batch job, such as notebooks or small fine-tuning runs, that need a guaranteed half of each of two GPUs and can grow to 80% when memory is free. Time-slicing gives each workload its own error domain, so a crash in one job doesn’t affect its neighbors. Running nvidia-smi in the container should show two GPUs, each with this workload’s fractional memory share. Getting started KAI Scheduler and the GPU Fractioning Operator are both on GitHub under the KAI Scheduler organization , with installation and configuration instructions for all three sharing mechanisms (See admin and user guides). Join the Slack channel or bi-weekly community meetings to ask your questions and contribute. For more information about CUDA 13.4, refer to the announcement. You can also get involved during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah , Nov. 9-12. Previously she worked on privacy implications of federated learning, focused on distributed training techniques and got fascinated by inefficiencies in GPU usage in research and industry settings. She established the AI Infrastructure Club and is based in Munich, Germany. View all posts by Ekin Karabulut About David Lifshitz David Lifshitz is a senior software engineer at NVIDIA, specializing in Kubernetes scheduling and GPU resource management for AI workloads. He is a maintainer of KAI Scheduler, an open-source CNCF Sandbox project that optimizes GPU resource allocation for AI and machine learning workloads. Previously at Run:ai, David helped develop the scheduling technology that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Drawing on his background in backend engineering, he focuses on building scalable systems that make efficient use of shared compute resources. View all posts by David Lifshitz About Hagay Sharon Hagay Sharon is a product manager with over two decades of experience, both in senior R&D and product management roles in areas of Networking, Cyber Security, and AI/ML products. Hagay joined NVIDIA as part of the Run:ai acquisition, where he serves as the product manager of Run:ai/KAI Scheduler, and Core GPU sharing areas. Hagay specializes in advanced Kubernetes AI scheduling, AI resources management, and GPU sharing technologies such as Run:ai fractions and SWAP technologies. His focus is on building sophisticated technological capabilities into the Run:ai/KAI product, turning them into end-user usable solutions and features. View all posts by Hagay Sharon Comments

It can be enabled when KAI is installed: helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \ -n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \ --set global.nvFractions.set=true This also installs gpu-fractioning as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations. There are four important annotations that answer four questions: 1. How much memory is needed 2. How far the workload may grow 3. How compute is shared 4. How many GPUs it spans How much memory: The request There are two ways to request memory: 1. As an absolute size: Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units: The container name ( app ) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container. 2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation: gpu-fraction: "0.5" How far it may grow: The limit This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request: Request Type Annotation Example Absolute Size nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit “80Gi” A Portion kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit “0.8” Table 2 : Which limit annotation to use for each type of memory request The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the gpu-fraction and less than 1. How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing Figure 1. Time-slicing divides the GPU’s time. SM-sharing divides its streaming multiprocessors (sm) Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together. Time-slicing is serial: Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation. SM-sharing is parallel: The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain. Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container: nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # or "time-slicing" A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs. How many GPUs are utilized To get fractional capacity on several devices, add: gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4" The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs. Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: inference labels: kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue annotations: nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi" nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi" # optional nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4" # optional, default 1 spec: schedulerName: kai-scheduler containers: - name: app image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04 This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together. Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default): metadata: annotations: gpu-fraction: "0.5" gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8" # optional nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "time-slicing" # optional gpu-fraction-num-devices: "2" # optional spec: schedulerName: kai-scheduler containers: - name: app This is an example for a development or batch job, such as notebooks or small fine-tuning runs, that need a guaranteed half of each of two GPUs and can grow to 80% when memory is free. Time-slicing gives each workload its own error domain, so a crash in one job doesn’t affect its neighbors. Running nvidia-smi in the container should show two GPUs, each with this workload’s fractional memory share. items.content: Back to Articles How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications Team Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 35 +29 Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows. Why Existing Solutions Fell Short Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations. They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. How We Solved It VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first. First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly. Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget. To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points. Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain. An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated. A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running. That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%. What Changed in the Grader To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime. The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810. Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version. The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter. Beyond the Grader To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling. VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803. Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe. Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary. The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon. Sources Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026). Gee, Leonidas, et al. " Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression ." EMNLP Industry Track (2022). Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023). Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. " In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs ." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026). The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter. Beyond the Grader To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling. VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803. Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe. Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary. The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon. items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.content: Back to Articles TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 32 +26 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron. Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx . New backend, native interface in HF libraries To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron . This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so. TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile . For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron. Transformers Inference Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices. The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations. import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401 from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B" MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024 PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512 dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) world_size = dist.get_world_size() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.bfloat16, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size), device_mesh=DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range (world_size))), ). eval () tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) if tokenizer.pad_token is None : tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token tokenizer.padding_side = "left" inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "The future of AI is" }], add_generation_prompt= True , padding= True , tokenizer_kwargs={ "pad_to_multiple_of" : PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE}, return_tensors= "pt" , ) generation_config = GenerationConfig( max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , use_cache= True , pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, cache_implementation= "static" , max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN, prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE, compile_config=CompileConfig(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= False , dynamic= False ), ) with torch.no_grad(): output_ids = model.generate( inputs[ "input_ids" ], attention_mask=inputs[ "attention_mask" ], generation_config=generation_config, ) if dist.get_rank() == 0 : prompt_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] print (tokenizer.decode(output_ids[ 0 , prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens= True )) Training Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings. Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer . If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar. import os import torch from datasets import load_dataset from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser def main ( script_args, training_args, model_args ): # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660) torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False training_args.model_init_kwargs = { "revision" : model_args.model_revision, "trust_remote_code" : training_args.trust_remote_code, "attn_implementation" : model_args.attn_implementation, "dtype" : model_args.dtype, "device_map" : None , } if int (os.environ.get( "WORLD_SIZE" , "1" )) > 1 : # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded training_args.model_init_kwargs[ "distributed_config" ] = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ.get( "TP_SIZE" , "1" )), fsdp_size= int (os.environ.get( "FSDP_SIZE" , "1" )), ) # Prepare dataset train_dataset = load_dataset( script_args.dataset_name, name=script_args.dataset_config, split=script_args.dataset_train_split, ) # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset. train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns([ "messages" ]) # Training trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model_args.model_name_or_path, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir) trainer.end() if __name__ == "__main__" : parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig)) script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config() main(script_args, training_args, model_args) Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs , SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained , and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config. Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium: Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure. Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 . The command below launches training with torchrun , which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node . The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups. TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \ --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \ --dataset_train_split train_sft \ --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max_length 2048 \ --packing true \ --packing_strategy wrapped \ --learning_rate 2e-5 \ --warmup_steps 0.03 \ --num_train_epochs 1 \ --logging_steps 2 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --save_only_model true \ --torch_compile true We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance. Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware. Diffusers Inference Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP: import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig # Distributed devices initialization dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) # TP dev = torch.neuron.current_device() mesh = DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range ( 8 ))) # TP=8 # Pipeline initialization model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1" transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( model, subfolder= "transformer" , torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP ) pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( model, transformer=transformer, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe.vae.to(dev) pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) # Image generation emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt= "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting" , device= "cpu" ) # text encoder stays on CPU image = pipe( prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev), prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None , height= 1024 , width= 1024 , num_inference_steps= 40 , generator=torch.Generator( "cpu" ).manual_seed( 0 ), # same noise on every rank ).images[ 0 ] if dist.get_rank() == 0 : image.save( "out.png" ) You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py . More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . Kernels Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub. You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium! Acknowledgments Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible. items.content: Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 6 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too.
