How to use the LFM3 models Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. LFM3-1.7B Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers : pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B" , trust_remote_code= True , ) messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is C. elegans?" }] output = generator( messages, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 2048 , ) print (output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ][ "content" ]) For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide . LFM3-VL-2B Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card . To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow Then load and run the model: import torch from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map= "auto" , trust_remote_code= True ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "url" : "https://placecats.com/300/200" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Describe this image." }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 16384 , # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True )[ 0 ]) See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp. LFM3-Audio-2B Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub: import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Respond with interleaved text and audio." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }]}, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "<|mixed_start|>" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, continue_final_message= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , audio_temperature= 1.0 , audio_top_k= 128 , audio_repetition_penalty= 1.1 , audio_repetition_window= 4096 , return_dict_in_generate= True , ) text = processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) waveform = codec.decode( outputs.audio_codes[: 1 , :, :outputs.audio_lengths[ 0 ]] ).audio_values[ 0 ] # 24 kHz print (text) sf.write( "reply.wav" , waveform. float ().cpu().numpy(), 24_000 ) See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B . Between the two d1 models: d1-2B : choose it for text, pictures, and video. It replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters and scores higher on all four of our decision suites, for example, 75.5 against 64.0 on ImajevBench. d1-omni-2B : choose it when your inputs include audio. To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass: import torch from transformers import AutoModel device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16 model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( "LiquidAI/d1-2B" , trust_remote_code= True , dtype=dtype).to(device) # Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass questions = { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer asking for a refund?" }, # yes/no: P(yes) "team" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Charges, refunds, invoices" , "shipping" : "Delivery and parcels" , "technical" : "App or site faults" }}, "topics" : { "type" : "choice" , "multiple" : True , "instructions" : "Which topics does the message raise?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and charges" , "delivery" : "Shipping and parcels" , "login" : "Signing in to the account" }}, "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is this ticket?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ]}, } out = model.system_one( "I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge." , questions) a = out[ "answers" ] urgency = a[ "urgency" ][ "legend" ][ str ( int (a[ "urgency" ][ "score" ]))] print ( round (a[ "refund" ][ "noul" ], 2 ), a[ "team" ][ "choice" ], a[ "topics" ][ "choices" ], urgency) # 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions. Fine-tune LFM3 for your task LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation. Model Method Task Notebook LFM3-1.7B SFT Extract structured JSON from messy documents Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B DPO Answer from retrieved documents, or decline Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B GRPO Call the right tools in a 108-tool phone app Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B CPT Learn a new language (Turkish) from raw text Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B SFT Read receipt photos into JSON Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B GRPO Transcribe images of equations to LaTeX Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Teach the model a new voice Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Answer spoken questions about medical images Open in Colab Example: teaching LFM3 to act We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation . The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware. Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video . Get Started with LFM3 All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: the LFM3 collection on Hugging Face, including LFM3-1.7B-Base for your own post-training. Fine-tune: adapt LFM3 to your task with our fine-tuning notebooks . Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. We can't wait to see what you build. Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model. How we built a more expressive backbone LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card . To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question about a photo by voice: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text." , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "photo.jpg" }, { "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , generation_mode= "text" ) print (processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:outputs.sequence_lengths[ 0 ]], skip_special_tokens= True , )) See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling. d1-2B and d1-omni-2B Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B . Between the two d1 models: d1-2B : choose it for text, pictures, and video. It replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters and scores higher on all four of our decision suites, for example, 75.5 against 64.0 on ImajevBench. d1-omni-2B : choose it when your inputs include audio. If you ask by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy. To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass: import torch from transformers import AutoModel device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16 model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( "LiquidAI/d1-2B" , trust_remote_code= True , dtype=dtype).to(device) # Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass questions = { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer asking for a refund?" }, # yes/no: P(yes) "team" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Charges, refunds, invoices" , "shipping" : "Delivery and parcels" , "technical" : "App or site faults" }}, "topics" : { "type" : "choice" , "multiple" : True , "instructions" : "Which topics does the message raise?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and charges" , "delivery" : "Shipping and parcels" , "login" : "Signing in to the account" }}, "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is this ticket?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ]}, } out = model.system_one( "I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge." , questions) a = out[ "answers" ] urgency = a[ "urgency" ][ "legend" ][ str ( int (a[ "urgency" ][ "score" ]))] print ( round (a[ "refund" ][ "noul" ], 2 ), a[ "team" ][ "choice" ], a[ "topics" ][ "choices" ], urgency) # 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions. Fine-tune LFM3 for your task LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation. Model Method Task Notebook LFM3-1.7B SFT Extract structured JSON from messy documents Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B DPO Answer from retrieved documents, or decline Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B GRPO Call the right tools in a 108-tool phone app Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B CPT Learn a new language (Turkish) from raw text Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B SFT Read receipt photos into JSON Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B GRPO Transcribe images of equations to LaTeX Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Teach the model a new voice Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Answer spoken questions about medical images Open in Colab Example: teaching LFM3 to act We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation . The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware. Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video . Get Started with LFM3 All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: the LFM3 collection on Hugging Face, including LFM3-1.7B-Base for your own post-training. Fine-tune: adapt LFM3 to your task with our fine-tuning notebooks . Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. We can't wait to see what you build. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.37658 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: When Should We Intervene at Test Time? Authors: Jiahao Zhang , Xinling Wen , Liangliang Li , Yu Chen View a PDF of the paper titled When Should We Intervene at Test Time?, by Jiahao Zhang and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Test-time adaptation helps a deployed model respond to changing inputs, but the same intervention can rescue one batch and damage the next. Updating normalization statistics, for example, can improve corrupted images yet fail when a batch contains mostly one class. Average accuracy hides these failures and cannot tell a model when to use an intervention. Target labels can guide this decision, but they are scarce and some choices are already clear. We introduce PORTAL, a controller that chooses when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying. Each available prediction rule is a candidate, and its predictions are fixed before current feedback arrives. Every acquired label therefore evaluates all candidates on the same input. PORTAL combines these shared comparisons and directs queries toward candidates that can still overtake the current leader. It stops when the remaining labels cannot change the choice or when the possible accuracy gain no longer justifies another query. Our analysis links the required feedback to accuracy gaps and shared mistakes, explaining why some choices need much less evidence. Experiments show that this control turns an intervention that loses accuracy overall into a useful choice on selected batches. It prevents severe failures caused by changes in arrival order and preserves gains across complete corruption streams. When a fixed rule already works well, PORTAL uses little feedback to retain its performance. Periodic label checks reveal when past evidence needs refreshing and help the controller recover as conditions change. The acquired labels also train stronger candidates for future batches, and selection brings nearly all of their accuracy gains into deployment. The same feedback therefore improves both the choice made now and the predictions available to later batches. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.37657 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness Authors: Igor Shilov , Xiaoxue Yang , Alexander Panfilov , Evgenii Kortukov , Matthieu Meeus , Peter Romov , Wojciech Samek , Jonas Geiping , Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye View a PDF of the paper titled Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness, by Igor Shilov and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions. items.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
items.summary: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness Abstract We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction–data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction–data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS.
items.content: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness Abstract We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction–data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction–data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 × 3\times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security–utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions. Igor Shilov ∗ 1 , Xiaoxue Yang ∗ 1 , Alexander Panfilov ∗ 2,3,4 Evgenii Kortukov 5 , Matthieu Meeus 1 , Peter Romov 1 , Wojciech Samek 5 Jonas Geiping † 2,3,4 , Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye † 1 1 Imperial College London 2 Tübingen AI Center 3 ELLIS Institute Tübingen 4 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 5 Fraunhofer HHI ∗ Equal contribution † Equal advising Website: imperial-aisp.github.io/heads_of_security Code: imperial-aisp/heads_of_security Demo: igorshilov/heads-of-security Models: imperial-cpg/heads-of-security 1 Introduction Indirect prompt injection ( Greshake et al., 2023 ) occurs when a model mistakes attacker-planted instructions in external content for authorized commands. As LLMs access more external data and tools, this attack surface becomes increasingly consequential. Although frontier models have become substantially harder to attack ( UK AI Security Institute, 2025 ) , prompt injection remains largely unsolved: adaptive attacks continue to succeed even against extensively evaluated systems ( Nasr et al., 2026 ; Andriushchenko et al., 2025 ) . This is more pronounced for open-weight models: under comparable red-teaming, Claude and GPT are substantially more robust than leading open-weight models ( Dziemian et al., 2026 ) . Defending against prompt injection requires several complementary mechanisms. We focus on instruction–data separation ( Zverev et al., 2025 ) , which creates a hard trust boundary: authorized instructions may steer model actions, while external data may be read and analyzed but not treated as instructions. Instruction–data separation applies when external content is intended as data, for example, when summarizing a webpage or extracting facts from a document. It complements other approaches such as instruction hierarchy ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) and contextual integrity ( Nissenbaum, 2004 ; Mireshghallah et al., 2024 ; Abdelnabi and Bagdasarian, 2026 ) by preventing attacks when a hard trust boundary exists. We propose H eads o f S ecurity (HoS), which enforces instruction–data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. These gates redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. HoS relies on two intuitions. First, previous interpretability works have shown that attention heads specialize in different functions, including in-context copying ( Elhage et al., 2021 ) , copy suppression ( McDougall et al., 2024 ) , and instruction following ( Hung et al., 2025 ) . This suggests that each head can learn its own redistribution of attention between trusted and untrusted content, specific to that head’s role, and that untrusted instructions can be suppressed without disrupting unrelated capabilities. Second, the trust boundary is supplied externally (e.g., web results are usually treated as untrusted), so enforcing it does not require the model to infer which sources are trusted or to acquire any new capabilities. Instead, it is an attention-routing problem: controlling how information from trusted and untrusted sources reaches the model’s existing capabilities. Figure 1: (Top) Heads of Security (HoS) learns to redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens. Green, red, and blue denote trusted, untrusted, and chat template tokens. Here, a head initially attends strongly to both the trusted request (“Count R’s”) and an injected instruction (“Send money”). Learned gates preserve trusted and chat template tokens ( × 1\!\times and × 0.9\!\times ) while suppressing untrusted tokens ( × 0.1\!\times ), shifting attention toward the trusted request. Gates are learned independently per head, so other heads may retain or increase attention to untrusted tokens. (Bottom) HoS improves security and utility. Compared to SecAlign and ASIDE, HoS is more robust against adaptive attacks (RL-Hammer and Claudini), better preserves utility across standard capability benchmarks, and achieves strong utility and security on static agentic benchmarks. We compare HoS against two defenses. SecAlign++ ( Chen et al., 2025c ) is a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense whose Meta-SecAlign-70B checkpoint is considered among the most adversarially robust open-weight models. ASIDE ( Zverev et al., 2026 ) is an architectural defense that enforces instruction–data separation by rotating the embeddings of untrusted content. We evaluate HoS on two open-weight models: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and GPT-OSS-20B ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . The former is a capable agentic model and the base model of Meta-SecAlign-70B, enabling direct comparison with SecAlign 1 1 1 For brevity, throughout this paper we use “SecAlign” to refer to the SecAlign++ training recipe. . GPT-OSS-20B is a newer, smaller mixture-of-experts reasoning model that has generally stronger capabilities than Llama-3.3-70B and has been post-trained to enforce instruction hierarchy. Compared to both SecAlign and ASIDE, HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. Greater robustness to adaptive attacks ( Section 4.1 ). Using black-box RL-based attacks trained with the RL-Hammer recipe ( Wen et al., 2025b ) , the strongest attackers reach 97% attack success rate (ASR) on GPT-OSS-20B, 85% on SecAlign, but only 10% on HoS. Similar results hold for Llama-3.3-70B: the strongest attacker reaches 99% ASR against the undefended model and 82% ASR against Meta-SecAlign-70B but only 1% ASR against HoS. In a white-box setting, a state-of-the-art optimization-based attack, Claudini ( Panfilov et al., 2026 ) , further optimized specifically against HoS in an autoresearch loop, still requires roughly 3 × 3\times more compute to reach 50% ASR on HoS compared to GPT-OSS-20B and its SecAlign variant. Preserving utility on standard benchmarks ( Section 4.2 ). Across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, HoS closely matches both base models. SecAlign and ASIDE match base-model performance in 0-shot evaluations but often struggle in few-shot and multi-turn settings. On 5-shot MMLU-Pro, HoS scores 67% versus GPT-OSS-20B’s 68%, while SecAlign and ASIDE fall to 59% and 52%; on Llama-3.3-70B, HoS scores 55% versus the base model’s 56%, while SecAlign falls to 16% ( Table 2 ). Strong utility and security on agentic benchmarks ( Section 4.3 , Appendix G ). On AgentDojo, AgentDyn, LLMail-Inject, and WASP, HoS and SecAlign perform comparably across both base models, substantially reducing ASR with little or no utility penalty in most evaluations ( Figure 4 , Table 3 ). On the other hand, ASIDE consistently fails to produce usable tool calls, scoring near-zero utility on three benchmarks and only 10% on AgentDojo. We also investigate what gates HoS learns mechanistically, using causal head ablations and role-confusion probes ( Section 5 ). Together, these results establish attention gating as a targeted and efficient approach to instruction–data separation. 2 Related work Prompt injection defenses. Various types of defenses have been proposed for instruction–data separation. Meta-SecAlign ( Chen et al., 2025c ) , our strongest baseline, is a finetuning-based method ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025c ) that uses DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) to teach models to follow user instructions while ignoring injections in data. Architectural methods directly encode input roles: Instructional Segment Embedding adds learned role embeddings to token embeddings ( Wu et al., 2025a ) , while ASIDE applies fixed rotations to data-token embeddings ( Zverev et al., 2026 ) . Our method, Heads of Security, also enforces instruction–data separation architecturally, but through reweighting attention according to token trust levels. Attention and prompt injection. Recent work suggests that the attention mechanism is directly related to instruction following. PASTA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and InstABoost ( Guardieiro et al., 2025 ) steer attention toward selected text or instruction tokens, while Causal Head Gating studies instruction-following mechanisms by suppressing attention head outputs ( Nam et al., 2025 ) . Under prompt injection, specific attention heads shift their attention from the benign instruction to injected instructions ( Hung et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) . HoS builds on these observations: we allow each head to learn its attention redistribution such that injected instructions are ignored. (Adaptive) attacks. Existing prompt injection defenses remain vulnerable, especially against strong adaptive attackers ( Nasr et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Panfilov et al., 2026 ) . RL-Hammer ( Wen et al., 2025b ) , a black-box RL-based attack, achieves ASRs of up to 92% against GPT-5-series models, 77% against Claude Sonnet 4, and near-100% on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct defended with SecAlign ( Chen et al., 2025c ) . This motivates our adaptive attack evaluations using RL and white-box optimization-based attacks developed by autoresearch ( Panfilov et al., 2026 ) . 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries We consider a decoder-only language model ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) consisting of L L transformer layers, each with h h attention heads of dimension d h d_{h} . The model receives a sequence of tokens t 1 , … , t n t_{1},\ldots,t_{n} and predicts a distribution over the next token t n + 1 t_{n+1} . On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security–utility trade-off over the base model. Igor Shilov ∗ 1 , Xiaoxue Yang ∗ 1 , Alexander Panfilov ∗ 2,3,4 Evgenii Kortukov 5 , Matthieu Meeus 1 , Peter Romov 1 , Wojciech Samek 5 Jonas Geiping † 2,3,4 , Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye † 1 1 Imperial College London 2 Tübingen AI Center 3 ELLIS Institute Tübingen 4 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 5 Fraunhofer HHI ∗ Equal contribution † Equal advising Website: imperial-aisp.github.io/heads_of_security Code: imperial-aisp/heads_of_security Demo: igorshilov/heads-of-security Models: imperial-cpg/heads-of-security 1 Introduction Indirect prompt injection ( Greshake et al., 2023 ) occurs when a model mistakes attacker-planted instructions in external content for authorized commands. As LLMs access more external data and tools, this attack surface becomes increasingly consequential. Although frontier models have become substantially harder to attack ( UK AI Security Institute, 2025 ) , prompt injection remains largely unsolved: adaptive attacks continue to succeed even against extensively evaluated systems ( Nasr et al., 2026 ; Andriushchenko et al., 2025 ) . This is more pronounced for open-weight models: under comparable red-teaming, Claude and GPT are substantially more robust than leading open-weight models ( Dziemian et al., 2026 ) . Defending against prompt injection requires several complementary mechanisms. We focus on instruction–data separation ( Zverev et al., 2025 ) , which creates a hard trust boundary: authorized instructions may steer model actions, while external data may be read and analyzed but not treated as instructions. Instruction–data separation applies when external content is intended as data, for example, when summarizing a webpage or extracting facts from a document. It complements other approaches such as instruction hierarchy ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) and contextual integrity ( Nissenbaum, 2004 ; Mireshghallah et al., 2024 ; Abdelnabi and Bagdasarian, 2026 ) by preventing attacks when a hard trust boundary exists. We propose H eads o f S ecurity (HoS), which enforces instruction–data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. These gates redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. HoS relies on two intuitions. First, previous interpretability works have shown that attention heads specialize in different functions, including in-context copying ( Elhage et al., 2021 ) , copy suppression ( McDougall et al., 2024 ) , and instruction following ( Hung et al., 2025 ) . This suggests that each head can learn its own redistribution of attention between trusted and untrusted content, specific to that head’s role, and that untrusted instructions can be suppressed without disrupting unrelated capabilities. Second, the trust boundary is supplied externally (e.g., web results are usually treated as untrusted), so enforcing it does not require the model to infer which sources are trusted or to acquire any new capabilities. Instead, it is an attention-routing problem: controlling how information from trusted and untrusted sources reaches the model’s existing capabilities. Figure 1: (Top) Heads of Security (HoS) learns to redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens. Green, red, and blue denote trusted, untrusted, and chat template tokens. Here, a head initially attends strongly to both the trusted request (“Count R’s”) and an injected instruction (“Send money”). Learned gates preserve trusted and chat template tokens ( × 1\!\times and × 0.9\!\times ) while suppressing untrusted tokens ( × 0.1\!\times ), shifting attention toward the trusted request. Gates are learned independently per head, so other heads may retain or increase attention to untrusted tokens. (Bottom) HoS improves security and utility. Compared to SecAlign and ASIDE, HoS is more robust against adaptive attacks (RL-Hammer and Claudini), better preserves utility across standard capability benchmarks, and achieves strong utility and security on static agentic benchmarks. We compare HoS against two defenses. SecAlign++ ( Chen et al., 2025c ) is a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense whose Meta-SecAlign-70B checkpoint is considered among the most adversarially robust open-weight models. ASIDE ( Zverev et al., 2026 ) is an architectural defense that enforces instruction–data separation by rotating the embeddings of untrusted content. We evaluate HoS on two open-weight models: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and GPT-OSS-20B ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . The former is a capable agentic model and the base model of Meta-SecAlign-70B, enabling direct comparison with SecAlign 1 1 1 For brevity, throughout this paper we use “SecAlign” to refer to the SecAlign++ training recipe. . GPT-OSS-20B is a newer, smaller mixture-of-experts reasoning model that has generally stronger capabilities than Llama-3.3-70B and has been post-trained to enforce instruction hierarchy. Compared to both SecAlign and ASIDE, HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. Greater robustness to adaptive attacks ( Section 4.1 ). Using black-box RL-based attacks trained with the RL-Hammer recipe ( Wen et al., 2025b ) , the strongest attackers reach 97% attack success rate (ASR) on GPT-OSS-20B, 85% on SecAlign, but only 10% on HoS. Similar results hold for Llama-3.3-70B: the strongest attacker reaches 99% ASR against the undefended model and 82% ASR against Meta-SecAlign-70B but only 1% ASR against HoS. In a white-box setting, a state-of-the-art optimization-based attack, Claudini ( Panfilov et al., 2026 ) , further optimized specifically against HoS in an autoresearch loop, still requires roughly 3 × 3\times more compute to reach 50% ASR on HoS compared to GPT-OSS-20B and its SecAlign variant. Preserving utility on standard benchmarks ( Section 4.2 ). Across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, HoS closely matches both base models. SecAlign and ASIDE match base-model performance in 0-shot evaluations but often struggle in few-shot and multi-turn settings. On 5-shot MMLU-Pro, HoS scores 67% versus GPT-OSS-20B’s 68%, while SecAlign and ASIDE fall to 59% and 52%; on Llama-3.3-70B, HoS scores 55% versus the base model’s 56%, while SecAlign falls to 16% ( Table 2 ). Strong utility and security on agentic benchmarks ( Section 4.3 , Appendix G ). On AgentDojo, AgentDyn, LLMail-Inject, and WASP, HoS and SecAlign perform comparably across both base models, substantially reducing ASR with little or no utility penalty in most evaluations ( Figure 4 , Table 3 ). On the other hand, ASIDE consistently fails to produce usable tool calls, scoring near-zero utility on three benchmarks and only 10% on AgentDojo. We also investigate what gates HoS learns mechanistically, using causal head ablations and role-confusion probes ( Section 5 ). Together, these results establish attention gating as a targeted and efficient approach to instruction–data separation. 2 Related work Prompt injection defenses. Various types of defenses have been proposed for instruction–data separation. Meta-SecAlign ( Chen et al., 2025c ) , our strongest baseline, is a finetuning-based method ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025c ) that uses DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) to teach models to follow user instructions while ignoring injections in data. Architectural methods directly encode input roles: Instructional Segment Embedding adds learned role embeddings to token embeddings ( Wu et al., 2025a ) , while ASIDE applies fixed rotations to data-token embeddings ( Zverev et al., 2026 ) . Our method, Heads of Security, also enforces instruction–data separation architecturally, but through reweighting attention according to token trust levels. Attention and prompt injection. Recent work suggests that the attention mechanism is directly related to instruction following. PASTA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and InstABoost ( Guardieiro et al., 2025 ) steer attention toward selected text or instruction tokens, while Causal Head Gating studies instruction-following mechanisms by suppressing attention head outputs ( Nam et al., 2025 ) . Under prompt injection, specific attention heads shift their attention from the benign instruction to injected instructions ( Hung et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) . HoS builds on these observations: we allow each head to learn its attention redistribution such that injected instructions are ignored. (Adaptive) attacks. Existing prompt injection defenses remain vulnerable, especially against strong adaptive attackers ( Nasr et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Panfilov et al., 2026 ) . RL-Hammer ( Wen et al., 2025b ) , a black-box RL-based attack, achieves ASRs of up to 92% against GPT-5-series models, 77% against Claude Sonnet 4, and near-100% on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct defended with SecAlign ( Chen et al., 2025c ) . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.37656 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops Authors: Aakash Sarkar , Ananya Mukherjee , Motoshige Sato View a PDF of the paper titled Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops, by Aakash Sarkar and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = \Psi(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $\Psi$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels. Comments: 7 pages, 1 figure. items.raw_text: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.37656 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops Authors: Aakash Sarkar , Ananya Mukherjee , Motoshige Sato View a PDF of the paper titled Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops, by Aakash Sarkar and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = \Psi(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $\Psi$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels. Comments: 7 pages, 1 figure. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.37648 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis Authors: Andrew Szot , Samira Abnar , Omar Attia , Abbas Kazerouni , Michael Kirchhof , Cheng-Yu Hsieh , Raviteja Vemulapalli , Alexander Toshev View a PDF of the paper titled Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis, by Andrew Szot and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks. items.content: \metadata [Correspondence] Andrew Szot: a_szot@apple.com Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis Andrew Szot Samira Abnar Omar Attia Abbas Kazerouni Michael Kirchhof Cheng-Yu Hsieh Raviteja Vemulapalli Alexander Toshev Affiliation: Apple October 27, 2026 Abstract We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI’s generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks. † † Apple and the Apple logo are trademarks of Apple Inc., registered in the U.S. and other countries and regions. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities as tool-use agents that interact with complex, stateful environments ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ) . Such agents must select and compose tools over multiple steps while tracking state changes and generalizing to new environments with new APIs. Progress in developing such agents depends on scaling high-quality, diverse training data. Yet producing this data is challenging because multi-step tool interactions are scarce in internet text and require realistic tasks, diverse tools, and rich environment data. Prior work addresses this challenge by using LLMs to synthesize tool-use data. While many existing works focus on synthesizing tool-use data to train stateless, read-only tool-use agents ( Schick et al., 2023 ) , work on scaling supervision for stateful tool-use agents is more limited. Some approaches use LLMs to synthesize entire tool-use trajectories, including simulating the tool responses ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Tang et al., 2023 ) . These techniques have demonstrated impressive scaling ( NVIDIA, 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , but complex tool outputs and state transitions can be difficult to simulate reliably. Other approaches synthesize code-backed executable tool environments ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . However, these efforts primarily emphasize increasing data quantity, leaving open which properties of the generated data drive downstream performance. Tool-use agent data varies in the diversity of available tools, the tasks they support, and the database states over which they operate. Understanding how these properties affect generalization is necessary to determine what data to generate as training scales. To study these relationships, we introduce SynthAPI, a controllable synthesis pipeline for multi-step tool-use environments. SynthAPI uses LLMs to implement apps comprising Python tools that read and modify structured databases. SynthAPI then generates tasks with initial database states, which we call data profiles and executable success verifiers. The key distinction from prior executable environment synthesis approaches is that SynthAPI provides explicit controls over the diversity of tools, tasks, and data profiles. These controls allow us to vary the composition of the synthesized training tasks and study how a fixed budget should be allocated among new tools, new tasks, and new data profiles. Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline and its controls. We use this controllability to derive a predictive scaling law that uses data composition factors to predict downstream tool-use agent generalization. We find that the data composition that best supports downstream generalization changes with scale. Comparisons at fixed task budgets show that, as these budgets grow, expanding tool diversity becomes more valuable than generating additional tasks within the same set of tools. Furthermore, repeating the same tasks with different data profiles also becomes more important than generating new tasks. Training with more complex data profiles also yields larger gains at higher budgets. These findings emphasize the importance of tool and data profile diversity over simply increasing the number of tasks. We propose an environment composition dependent scaling law that captures these effects. Across four model sizes, we hold out the runs in the top 25% of training FLOPs and show that the law extrapolates to them, including runs with up to 16 × 16\times the largest FLOP budget used for fitting, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.0285 0.0285 on the normalized downstream score, compared with 0.1706 0.1706 for a scaling model that relies on the number of tasks alone and ignores the composition of environment properties. With the optimal environment composition recipe determined by our proposed method, we show SynthAPI transfers to broad tool-use agent benchmarks across AppWorld, BFCL, and ASTRA-Bench ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ; Xiu et al., 2026 ) . At a fixed data budget, the recipe identified by our analysis outperforms a suboptimal recipe that simply relies on scaling the number of tasks alone across all model sizes and benchmarks. We find that agents trained on the SynthAPI data outperform agents trained on prior large-scale tool-use agent data ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) by 30.5 30.5 percentage points on average across the three benchmarks. We also compare SynthAPI to strong per-benchmark data synthesis baselines, outperforming the strongest baseline at each model size by 7.6 7.6 – 11.6 11.6 percentage points on AppWorld Test-Challenge and 2.0 2.0 – 3.7 3.7 points on BFCL ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . These results demonstrate the importance of properly scaling the data composition of synthesized environments through our scaling law enabled by the controllable environment generation in SynthAPI. Figure 1 : Overview of SynthAPI. On the left, we show the tool-use agent tasks we focus on, where given an instruction, an agent must reason and execute tool calls to complete the task. In the middle, the SynthAPI pipeline generates synthetic tool-use agent environments at scale. SynthAPI generates this data while controlling the diversity of the tools, tasks, and starting database states. These controls allow deriving the scaling laws on the right (presented in detail in Figure 3 ). 2 Related Work Synthetic supervision has been widely used to train LLMs for tool use. Early methods train on demonstrations over predefined API collections ( Schick et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent work generates supervision through live APIs and executable functions ( Liu et al., 2024b ; Prabhakar et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches simulate API responses with LLMs ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Tang et al., 2023 ) or combine data from multiple sources and synthesis pipelines ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . DIVE ( Chen et al., 2026 ) analyzes tool diversity in evidence-based question answering, whereas SynthAPI studies multi-step read-write workflows over structured databases, a setting emphasized by recent tool-use agent benchmarks ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ) . Nemotron-Agentic ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) scales LLM-simulated tool interactions to 335k trajectories. SimSAT ( Lee et al., 2026 ) extends such simulation to long-horizon tasks. However, these simulators rely on an LLM to generate every tool response, making increasingly complex outputs and state transitions difficult to simulate reliably. Thus, unlike these works, SynthAPI scales tool data through database-backed executable environments. Like SynthAPI, recent work also synthesizes executable tool-use environments backed by persistent databases ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . Unlike these works, SynthAPI couples this synthesis with explicit controls over the diversity and complexity of tools, task instructions, and initial database states. These controls let us disentangle how training-data composition affects downstream generalization. Our analysis goes beyond prior scaling studies that primarily vary the number of synthesized environments or examine domain diversity at a fixed task count ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, we study how to allocate a fixed data budget among new tools, additional tasks for existing tools, and alternative database states for existing tasks. We further derive a joint scaling law that extrapolates aggregate downstream generalization to larger compute budgets and predicts which data allocations maximize performance. We use these predictions to design a training recipe that improves agent performance over prior synthetic-data generation approaches. Scaling laws characterize predictable relationships between model quality, model size, data volume, and training compute. Early work established power-law behavior in language-model pre-training, while compute-optimal analyses studied how a fixed budget should be divided between parameters and tokens ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Related studies extend scaling analysis to transfer learning, fine-tuning, and reinforcement-learning post-training ( Hernandez et al., 2021 ; Tan et al., 2025 ) . For tool-use models, prior work develops scaling laws for pre-training with agent data, using benchmark loss as the prediction target ( Zhuang et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, SynthAPI predicts downstream task success from environment-generation factors, relating generalization to the scale, and diversity of generated tools, tasks, and data profiles. 3 SynthAPI: Synthetic Environments for Tool-Use Agents SynthAPI is a controllable pipeline for synthesizing interactive tool-use agent environments. SynthAPI consists of two stages where first apps consisting of APIs and databases are coded in Python and next tasks are constructed using the functionality in these apps. 3.1 API Generation In the first phase of creating synthetic tool-use agent tasks, SynthAPI generates a wide diversity of tools to base tasks on. SynthAPI does this by synthesizing “apps”, which are a coherent collection of interacting tools that can be composed to solve realistic tasks. This organization naturally produces dependencies among tools and mirrors deployment settings in which agents use tools to accomplish user goals. These apps are each independently implemented in Python code from scratch by an LLM, which we term the “builder LLM”. We use Gemini-3.1 Pro ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) with internet access disabled as the builder LLM. We manually define a broad app taxonomy consisting of shopping, music, productivity, finance, fitness, messaging, utilities, and social. The builder LLM starts to generate an app by generating “metadata” consisting of the app name, a short app description, the taxonomy category the app belongs to, and a list of functionalities. The functionalities are short descriptions of interactions possible in the app, such as “Initiate a return” or “Apply a promo code to your shopping cart” in the case of a shopping app. Next, SynthAPI generates a database schema for the app from the metadata to ground app functionality in complex stateful interactions. For example, in a shopping app there need to be products, inventory, users, addresses, payment methods, reviews, carts, and orders for the tools in the app to implement meaningful behaviors. Given the app metadata, the builder LLM generates a db.py file that contains Python Enum and dataclass definitions defining all data types necessary to instantiate the provided app functionalities. These classes only specify data formats rather than instantiated database states. The final step of app creation is generating an API layer that operates on the database schema. From the contents of db.py and the app metadata, the builder LLM generates an apis.py file for the app. The API file consists of a set of Python functions defining the possible operations in the app. Each function takes as input a database object that tracks instantiated data schema objects, along with any other input arguments, which may consist of the defined data types. These functions read or modify instantiated database objects and collectively define the agent’s available tools. In a shopping app, example resulting APIs may search products, inspect reviewers, or create an order. Public functions from the API set are exposed to the agent as callable tools. In summary, in the first phase, SynthAPI generates a set of apps, each of which contains app metadata, a data schema Python file, and an API definition file. All components are generated from scratch by the builder LLM. See Section A.1 for all details and prompts on app generation. 3.2 Task Generation The apps specify which tools and data schemas are possible for the agent to interact with, but they do not specify actual tasks to complete. The second phase of SynthAPI therefore synthesizes actionable tasks for agents to complete using the provided APIs. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI’s generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks. † † Apple and the Apple logo are trademarks of Apple Inc., registered in the U.S. and other countries and regions. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities as tool-use agents that interact with complex, stateful environments ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ) . Such agents must select and compose tools over multiple steps while tracking state changes and generalizing to new environments with new APIs. Progress in developing such agents depends on scaling high-quality, diverse training data. Yet producing this data is challenging because multi-step tool interactions are scarce in internet text and require realistic tasks, diverse tools, and rich environment data. Prior work addresses this challenge by using LLMs to synthesize tool-use data. While many existing works focus on synthesizing tool-use data to train stateless, read-only tool-use agents ( Schick et al., 2023 ) , work on scaling supervision for stateful tool-use agents is more limited. Some approaches use LLMs to synthesize entire tool-use trajectories, including simulating the tool responses ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Tang et al., 2023 ) . These techniques have demonstrated impressive scaling ( NVIDIA, 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , but complex tool outputs and state transitions can be difficult to simulate reliably. Other approaches synthesize code-backed executable tool environments ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . However, these efforts primarily emphasize increasing data quantity, leaving open which properties of the generated data drive downstream performance. Tool-use agent data varies in the diversity of available tools, the tasks they support, and the database states over which they operate. Understanding how these properties affect generalization is necessary to determine what data to generate as training scales. To study these relationships, we introduce SynthAPI, a controllable synthesis pipeline for multi-step tool-use environments. SynthAPI uses LLMs to implement apps comprising Python tools that read and modify structured databases. SynthAPI then generates tasks with initial database states, which we call data profiles and executable success verifiers. The key distinction from prior executable environment synthesis approaches is that SynthAPI provides explicit controls over the diversity of tools, tasks, and data profiles. These controls allow us to vary the composition of the synthesized training tasks and study how a fixed budget should be allocated among new tools, new tasks, and new data profiles. Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline and its controls. We use this controllability to derive a predictive scaling law that uses data composition factors to predict downstream tool-use agent generalization. We find that the data composition that best supports downstream generalization changes with scale. Comparisons at fixed task budgets show that, as these budgets grow, expanding tool diversity becomes more valuable than generating additional tasks within the same set of tools. Furthermore, repeating the same tasks with different data profiles also becomes more important than generating new tasks. Training with more complex data profiles also yields larger gains at higher budgets. These findings emphasize the importance of tool and data profile diversity over simply increasing the number of tasks. We propose an environment composition dependent scaling law that captures these effects. Across four model sizes, we hold out the runs in the top 25% of training FLOPs and show that the law extrapolates to them, including runs with up to 16 × 16\times the largest FLOP budget used for fitting, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.0285 0.0285 on the normalized downstream score, compared with 0.1706 0.1706 for a scaling model that relies on the number of tasks alone and ignores the composition of environment properties. With the optimal environment composition recipe determined by our proposed method, we show SynthAPI transfers to broad tool-use agent benchmarks across AppWorld, BFCL, and ASTRA-Bench ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ; Xiu et al., 2026 ) . At a fixed data budget, the recipe identified by our analysis outperforms a suboptimal recipe that simply relies on scaling the number of tasks alone across all model sizes and benchmarks. We find that agents trained on the SynthAPI data outperform agents trained on prior large-scale tool-use agent data ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) by 30.5 30.5 percentage points on average across the three benchmarks. We also compare SynthAPI to strong per-benchmark data synthesis baselines, outperforming the strongest baseline at each model size by 7.6 7.6 – 11.6 11.6 percentage points on AppWorld Test-Challenge and 2.0 2.0 – 3.7 3.7 points on BFCL ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . These results demonstrate the importance of properly scaling the data composition of synthesized environments through our scaling law enabled by the controllable environment generation in SynthAPI. Figure 1 : Overview of SynthAPI. On the left, we show the tool-use agent tasks we focus on, where given an instruction, an agent must reason and execute tool calls to complete the task. In the middle, the SynthAPI pipeline generates synthetic tool-use agent environments at scale. SynthAPI generates this data while controlling the diversity of the tools, tasks, and starting database states. These controls allow deriving the scaling laws on the right (presented in detail in Figure 3 ). 2 Related Work Synthetic supervision has been widely used to train LLMs for tool use. Early methods train on demonstrations over predefined API collections ( Schick et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent work generates supervision through live APIs and executable functions ( Liu et al., 2024b ; Prabhakar et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches simulate API responses with LLMs ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Tang et al., 2023 ) or combine data from multiple sources and synthesis pipelines ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . DIVE ( Chen et al., 2026 ) analyzes tool diversity in evidence-based question answering, whereas SynthAPI studies multi-step read-write workflows over structured databases, a setting emphasized by recent tool-use agent benchmarks ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ) . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.37655 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry Authors: Wenqing Peng , Michael Boy , Zhi-Song Liu View a PDF of the paper titled KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry, by Wenqing Peng and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the \texttt{diffrax} library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30\% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4--5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics--machine-learning modelling.
