items.content: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry Wenqing Peng † † thanks: Corresponding author: wenqing.peng@helsinki.fi Affiliation: Institute for Atmospheric and Earth Systems Research, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland Affiliation: Atmospheric Modelling Centre Lahti (AMC-Lahti), Lahti, Finland Michael Boy Affiliation: Institute for Atmospheric and Earth Systems Research, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland Affiliation: LUT University, Department of Computational Engineering, Lahti, Finland Affiliation: Atmospheric Modelling Centre Lahti (AMC-Lahti), Lahti, Finland Zhi-Song Liu Affiliation: LUT University, Department of Computational Engineering, Lahti, Finland Affiliation: Atmospheric Modelling Centre Lahti (AMC-Lahti), Lahti, Finland Abstract Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the diffrax library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4–5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics–machine-learning modelling. 1 Introduction Chemicals and aerosols in the ambient air affect human health, weather, and climate ( Seinfeld and Pandis, 2016 ) . Their atmospheric concentrations vary strongly in space and time, governed by emission, chemical transformation, aerosol formation, transport by meteorological conditions, and eventual removal by deposition ( Brasseur and Jacob, 2017 ) . Comprehensive atmospheric chemical mechanisms, such as the near-explicit Master Chemical Mechanism ( Jenkin et al., 1997 ; Saunders et al., 2003 ) , contain thousands of species coupled through more than ten thousand reactions, and hand-coding the resulting stiff ODE system and its Jacobian is tedious and error-prone. The Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP) automates this process ( Damian et al., 2002 ) . Given a chemical mechanism specified in a dedicated description syntax, the KPP language, KPP parses the reaction list with a Flex/Yacc scanner–parser and generates Fortran or C code that evaluates the time derivative of the concentrations and its Jacobian. The generated code exploits the sparsity of the Jacobian through species reordering and sparse linear algebra routines, which keeps the implicit time stepping required by stiff chemistry efficient, and it is paired with a suite of stiff numerical integrators, including Rosenbrock, BDF, and Runge–Kutta methods. KPP also generates direct-decoupled and adjoint sensitivity code, which efficiently computes derivatives of the model solution with respect to rate coefficients, initial concentrations, and other parameters. These sensitivities support applications such as parameter estimation, uncertainty analysis, and variational data assimilation ( Sandu et al., 2003 ) . This tight coupling between mechanism parsing, sparse Jacobian generation, and forward and adjoint sensitivity code generation has made KPP a standard tool in atmospheric chemistry modelling, but it also means that the resulting code inherits the constraints of the Fortran and C environments and of the CPU hardware for which it was designed. Other tools to preprocess and solve chemical kinetics have been developed for other software and hardware environments. pykpp ( Henderson, ) is a preprocessor written in Python, which parses mechanisms written in the KPP language and solves the kinetic ODE with SciPy solvers. PyBox generates 0-dimensional box models that include both atmospheric chemistry and aerosol processes, in which the chemistry is solved by the Assimulo ODE solver ( Topping et al., 2018 ) , and PyCHAM reuses the mechanism parsing of PyBox but solves the ODE with SciPy ( O’Meara et al., 2021 ) . The Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols (MUSICA) is implemented in C++ and provides an option to run on accelerators such as GPUs ( Pfister et al., 2020 ) . For the EMAC model, a source-to-source tool translates the KPP-generated Fortran code into CUDA kernels to solve the chemical kinetics on GPUs ( Alvanos and Christoudias, 2017 ) . TChem-atm couples gas-phase and aerosol chemistry and runs on CPUs and GPUs through the Kokkos performance-portability library, constructing the Jacobian automatically for a range of stiff ODE solvers ( Díaz-Ibarra et al., 2026 ) . These developments target the efficient forward simulation of process-based atmospheric models, which are built on explicit physical and chemical processes and are therefore interpretable, since the driving forces in the model can be perturbed to test their influence on the output. However, process-based models are limited by the processes that they do not resolve, and amending the model structure or tuning its parameters against observations remains laborious and computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches, for example neural networks trained on historical atmospheric observations, offer flexible and fast emulation of atmospheric processes with comparable accuracy. ChemNNE is a neural-network emulator of the atmospheric chemical ODE that is considerably faster than the numerical solver ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and TopoFlow is a topography-aware neural network for high-resolution air-quality prediction ( Kheder et al., 2026 ) . Neural networks can also partially solve the estimation of rate coefficients in chemical ODEs ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, purely data-driven models often lack interpretability and the ability to predict anomalies or extreme events, and their training is data-intensive and becomes infeasible when observations are sparse. Neural networks are trained by gradient descent, which relies on automatic differentiation, and although this is possible in Fortran, the majority of neural-network models are developed in Julia or in Python frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX. Hybrid models that combine physically based process models with data-driven neural networks are expected to unite the flexibility of neural networks with the interpretability and physical constraints of process-based models, enabling both fast emulation and learning from data and an understanding of the underlying processes ( Shen et al., 2023 ; Innes et al., 2019 ; Gelbrecht et al., 2023 ) . For example, the hybrid weather and climate model NeuralGCM, which combines a differentiable dynamical core with neural networks, both implemented in JAX, achieves a performance comparable to the best machine-learning and process-based models ( Kochkov et al., 2024 ) . In ecohydrology, JAX-CanVeg integrates a land-surface model with neural-network components and improves the simulation ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Such hybrid models require the process model itself to be differentiable, so that gradients can be propagated through it to the network parameters. General-purpose differentiable modelling tools for reaction networks exist, such as Catalyst.jl in Julia ( Loman et al., 2023 ) , but to the best of our knowledge no tool generates differentiable code from mechanisms written in the KPP language, in which atmospheric mechanisms such as the MCM are distributed and used. Differentiability matters most for inverse problems, in which model parameters or inputs are inferred from observations of the model output. Estimating rate coefficients from chamber or flow-tube observations is such a problem, and it is often ill-posed because the observations constrain only some combinations of the rate coefficients, so that the identifiability of the parameters should be analysed before they are estimated ( Guillaume et al., 2019 ) . Another example is the inversion of emissions from concentration observations, which has traditionally relied on variational data assimilation with hand-derived adjoint models ( Elbern et al., 2007 ; Henze et al., 2007 ) . To learn how emissions depend on environmental drivers, the retrieved emission fields can be used to train a neural network offline, in the same way as data assimilation has been combined with machine learning to learn model dynamics from sparse and noisy observations ( Brajard et al., 2020 ) . Such a two-step approach, however, discards the information that the individual retrievals cannot resolve, whereas online training, in which the network is fitted to the observations through the chemical model, requires the gradient of the model output with respect to the network parameters. To address this, we present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor implemented in the JAX framework that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code from mechanisms written in the KPP language, which is directly usable within the data-driven modelling ecosystem. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the diffrax library ( Kidger, 2022 ) , which enables inverse modelling, parameter estimation, and hybrid modelling of physical and neural models. Section 2 describes the implementation. Section 3 uses the sensitivities from KPPax to analyse the identifiability of the rate coefficients of a benchmark mechanism before estimating them from noisy synthetic observations. Section 4 trains a neural-network correction of an emission inventory and shows that online fine-tuning through the chemical model improves on the offline two-step approach. Section 5 discusses the limitations, and Sect. 6 concludes. 2 Implementation of differentiable kinetic pre-processing 2.1 The chemistry kinetic problem An atmospheric chemical reaction system can be mathematically formulated by a coupled system of stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Consider a reaction system of n species and m reactions. We denote the concentration of species i i as y i y_{i} and reaction j j as r j r_{j} , with 1 ≤ i ≤ n , 1 ≤ j ≤ m 1\leq i\leq n,1\leq j\leq m . Let 𝒚 = [ y 1 , … , y n ] T \bm{y}=[y_{1},...,y_{n}]^{T} be a vector of concentration of all the species. The stoichiometric coefficients define the quantitative relationship of the reactants and the products involved in the reaction. We define the stoichiometric coefficient s i , j − s_{i,j}^{-} as the number of molecules of species i i that react and consumed in the reaction j j , and similarly s i , j + s_{i,j}^{+} as the number of molecules produced. The reaction j j can be generically formulated as: ∑ s i , j − ​ y i → ∑ s i , j + ​ y i \sum s_{i,j}^{-}y_{i}\xrightarrow{}\sum s_{i,j}^{+}y_{i} (1) The kinetic reaction rate law define the reaction rate ω j \omega_{j} of the reaction j j as a proportion with the multiplication of the concentration of the reactants raised by the partial order for reactant s i , j − s_{i,j}^{-} , with the proportionality constant defined as the rate coefficient (rate constant) k j k_{j} : ω j ​ ( t , 𝒚 ) = k j ​ ( t ) ​ ∏ i = 1 n y i s i , j − \omega_{j}(t,\bm{y})=k_{j}(t)\prod_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}^{s_{i,j}^{-}} (2) Depending on the reaction system, the rate coefficient may be either a constant or a time-dependent quantity that varies with environmental conditions. For instance, the photolysis rate of NO 3 depends on the actinic flux (light intensity), while the rate of cross-reactions among intermediate peroxy radicals depends on the total concentration of peroxy radicals present in the system. The KPP language, developed by the KPP project, consists of sections, commands, and inline codes. KPP sections contain the description of reaction schemes, including the species and reactions. KPP commands control the code generation and the behaviour of the generated code. More custom behaviour can be implemented as inline code, and be inserted into a certain location in the generated code. KPPax uses only the sections that describe the mechanism, i.e. the species and the equations, because its objective is to generate the chemistry code alone, and it is the responsibility of the user to provide the initial concentrations and to construct the customised simulation. Following the taxonomy of reaction parsing in ( Damian et al., 2002 ) , KPPax parses the kinetic equations in a mixture of the totally integrated approach and the preprocessing approach. The former parses the chemical mechanism once into a set of coefficient arrays that are subsequently evaluated by generic array operations at run time, and the latter generates mechanism-specific source code ahead of time, as KPP itself does. We utilise the parsing module from pykpp , which defines and parse the KPP language using the pyparsing module and returns a list of reactions composed of reactants, products, and rate coefficient expression. The stoichiometric coefficients are converted into sparse array literals in the coordinate list (COO) format, with row/column indices and values stored in separate arrays ( 𝒊 , 𝒋 , 𝒗 ) (\bm{i},\bm{j},\bm{v}) . The time dependent rate coefficients are converted from Fortran expression to JAX expression and wrapped as a python function. To exploit the computational power of accelerators, we implement the rate law in fully sparse matrix operation. Rather than materialising 𝑺 − \bm{S}^{-} and 𝑺 \bm{S} as dense matrices, the rate law (Eq. 2 - 4 ) is evaluated directly from their COO representation using index-gather and segment-reduction primitives, as summarised in Algorithm 1 . The reactant product term in Eq. 2 is computed as a segment product: partial powers y i s i , j − y_{i}^{s_{i,j}^{-}} are gathered at the non-zero row indices of 𝑺 − \bm{S}^{-} and reduced onto the reaction axis j j by scatter-multiplication. Algorithm 1 Sparse evaluation of the rate law 0: 𝒚 \bm{y} ; 𝒌 \bm{k} ; 𝑺 − \bm{S}^{-} : ( 𝒊 r , 𝒋 r , 𝒗 r ) (\bm{i}_{r},\bm{j}_{r},\bm{v}_{r}) ; 𝑺 \bm{S} : ( 𝒊 s , 𝒋 s , 𝒗 s ) (\bm{i}_{s},\bm{j}_{s},\bm{v}_{s}) 1: 𝒑 ← 𝒚 ​ [ 𝒊 r ] 𝒗 r \bm{p}\leftarrow\bm{y}[\bm{i}_{r}]^{\,\bm{v}_{r}} {gather and raise to partial order} 2: 𝝎 ← 𝒌 ⊙ segment ​ _ ​ prod ​ ( 𝒑 , 𝒋 r ) \bm{\omega}\leftarrow\bm{k}\odot\mathrm{segment\_prod}(\bm{p},\bm{j}_{r}) {scatter-multiply onto reaction axis} 3: 𝒚 ˙ ← segment ​ _ ​ sum ​ ( 𝒗 s ⊙ 𝝎 ⁡ [ 𝒋 s ] , 𝒊 s ) \dot{\bm{y}}\leftarrow\mathrm{segment\_sum}(\bm{v}_{s}\odot\bm{\omega}[\bm{j}_{s}],\,\bm{i}_{s}) {scatter-add onto species axis} 4: return 𝒚 ˙ \dot{\bm{y}} This power-multiply formulation is not differentiable in practice, because the reactant product is realised as a scatter-multiplication over repeated reaction indices, for which JAX does not implement a differentiation rule. Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are numerically stiff, because reactive radical species relax on timescales of milliseconds to seconds, while longer-lived species evolve over hours, so the system’s Jacobian eigenvalues span many orders of magnitude. Explicit integration schemes are constrained by this stiffness to prohibitively small time steps for stability, rather than accuracy, and are therefore unsuitable, which is why KPP itself provides implicit and Rosenbrock-type solvers ( Sandu et al., 2003 ) . We integrate Eq. ( 4 ) using diffrax ( Kidger, 2022 ) , a JAX-native library of differentiable ODE solvers, selecting the implicit Kvaerno family of solvers, which combine embedded error estimates with an implicit treatment of the stiff terms via a diagonally implicit Runge-Kutta scheme, avoiding the step-size collapse of explicit methods. Step size is controlled adaptively by a proportional-integral (PID) controller, which adjusts d ​ t \mathrm{d}t to meet a prescribed local error tolerance rather than relying on a fixed or manually tuned step size. Because concentrations must remain strictly positive for the log-space rate law (Eq. 6 ), we additionally clip y y to a small positive floor at each evaluation of the right-hand side, preventing the solver from probing negative or exactly zero concentrations during error-controlled step adjustment. We perform all stiff ODE integration in 64-bit double precision. 2.3 Automatic differentiation Automatic differentiation (AD) computes exact derivatives of a numerical program by decomposing it into elementary operations and applying the chain rule systematically, either forward alongside the primal computation (forward mode) or backward from the output (reverse mode). Once the rate law and its numerical integration are expressed as JAX-traceable array operations, the sensitivity of an output quantity, for instance an observed concentration at time t F t_{F} , with respect to an input quantity, for instance an emission rate or a rate coefficient, can therefore be obtained automatically, without deriving the corresponding tangent-linear or adjoint equations by hand. Differentiating through an ODE solve is nonetheless a distinct problem from differentiating a single expression, since the numerical solution is produced by an iterative sequence of solver steps rather than a closed-form function. Two broad strategies exist for obtaining the required sensitivities, namely the optimize-then-discretize adjoint, which derives an adjoint ODE from the continuous forward equations and integrates it backwards independently of how the forward solve was discretised, and the discretize-then-optimize adjoint, which differentiates the forward numerical scheme itself, step by step, yielding the exact gradient of the numerical solution rather than an approximation to the gradient of the underlying continuous problem ( Sandu et al., 2003 ) . KPP implements both, but its discretize-then-optimize adjoint must be derived analytically for each integrator in turn. For example, Sandu et al. (2003) derive it explicitly for the linearly implicit Euler method, requiring not only the Jacobian but also its derivative with respect to concentration (the Hessian tensor) and dedicated sparse linear-algebra routines to evaluate it efficiently. They note this construction to be considerably more demanding than their optimize-then-discretize adjoint, and correspondingly, KPP provides hand-derived discretize-then-optimize adjoints for only a subset of its integrators. diffrax ( Kidger, 2022 ) instead obtains a discretize-then-optimize adjoint of the forward solve through reverse-mode AD applied directly to the solver’s internal steps, exposing the differentiation strategy as a configurable component of the solve rather than a property fixed by the choice of integrator. Naively differentiating through every accepted step this way would require storing each intermediate solver state, incurring memory cost proportional to the number of steps. The recursive checkpoint adjoint avoids this by checkpointing only a logarithmic subset of states and recomputing the remainder on demand during the backward pass, keeping memory cost sub-linear in step count while still returning the exact discrete gradient. Because this adjoint is generated automatically for any solver JAX can trace, KPPax removes the need to derive a Hessian or a solver-specific adjoint step by hand for every integrator, and with it the correctness risk that Sandu et al. (2003) themselves highlight for hand-written or general-purpose adjoint-compiler code. The trade-off is computational rather than conceptual: checkpointed recomputation adds cost that a hand-derived discretize-then-optimize adjoint, once implemented, would not incur, particularly for very large mechanisms. We consider this an acceptable exchange for the substantial reduction in implementation and maintenance effort it affords when extending KPPax to new mechanisms or integrators. 3 Application I: identifiability and parameter estimation Rate coefficients of atmospheric chem

The Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols (MUSICA) is implemented in C++ and provides an option to run on accelerators such as GPUs ( Pfister et al., 2020 ) . For the EMAC model, a source-to-source tool translates the KPP-generated Fortran code into CUDA kernels to solve the chemical kinetics on GPUs ( Alvanos and Christoudias, 2017 ) . TChem-atm couples gas-phase and aerosol chemistry and runs on CPUs and GPUs through the Kokkos performance-portability library, constructing the Jacobian automatically for a range of stiff ODE solvers ( Díaz-Ibarra et al., 2026 ) . These developments target the efficient forward simulation of process-based atmospheric models, which are built on explicit physical and chemical processes and are therefore interpretable, since the driving forces in the model can be perturbed to test their influence on the output. However, process-based models are limited by the processes that they do not resolve, and amending the model structure or tuning its parameters against observations remains laborious and computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches, for example neural networks trained on historical atmospheric observations, offer flexible and fast emulation of atmospheric processes with comparable accuracy. ChemNNE is a neural-network emulator of the atmospheric chemical ODE that is considerably faster than the numerical solver ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and TopoFlow is a topography-aware neural network for high-resolution air-quality prediction ( Kheder et al., 2026 ) . Neural networks can also partially solve the estimation of rate coefficients in chemical ODEs ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, purely data-driven models often lack interpretability and the ability to predict anomalies or extreme events, and their training is data-intensive and becomes infeasible when observations are sparse. Neural networks are trained by gradient descent, which relies on automatic differentiation, and although this is possible in Fortran, the majority of neural-network models are developed in Julia or in Python frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX. Hybrid models that combine physically based process models with data-driven neural networks are expected to unite the flexibility of neural networks with the interpretability and physical constraints of process-based models, enabling both fast emulation and learning from data and an understanding of the underlying processes ( Shen et al., 2023 ; Innes et al., 2019 ; Gelbrecht et al., 2023 ) . For example, the hybrid weather and climate model NeuralGCM, which combines a differentiable dynamical core with neural networks, both implemented in JAX, achieves a performance comparable to the best machine-learning and process-based models ( Kochkov et al., 2024 ) . In ecohydrology, JAX-CanVeg integrates a land-surface model with neural-network components and improves the simulation ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Such hybrid models require the process model itself to be differentiable, so that gradients can be propagated through it to the network parameters. General-purpose differentiable modelling tools for reaction networks exist, such as Catalyst.jl in Julia ( Loman et al., 2023 ) , but to the best of our knowledge no tool generates differentiable code from mechanisms written in the KPP language, in which atmospheric mechanisms such as the MCM are distributed and used. Differentiability matters most for inverse problems, in which model parameters or inputs are inferred from observations of the model output. Estimating rate coefficients from chamber or flow-tube observations is such a problem, and it is often ill-posed because the observations constrain only some combinations of the rate coefficients, so that the identifiability of the parameters should be analysed before they are estimated ( Guillaume et al., 2019 ) . Another example is the inversion of emissions from concentration observations, which has traditionally relied on variational data assimilation with hand-derived adjoint models ( Elbern et al., 2007 ; Henze et al., 2007 ) . To learn how emissions depend on environmental drivers, the retrieved emission fields can be used to train a neural network offline, in the same way as data assimilation has been combined with machine learning to learn model dynamics from sparse and noisy observations ( Brajard et al., 2020 ) . Such a two-step approach, however, discards the information that the individual retrievals cannot resolve, whereas online training, in which the network is fitted to the observations through the chemical model, requires the gradient of the model output with respect to the network parameters. To address this, we present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor implemented in the JAX framework that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code from mechanisms written in the KPP language, which is directly usable within the data-driven modelling ecosystem. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the diffrax library ( Kidger, 2022 ) , which enables inverse modelling, parameter estimation, and hybrid modelling of physical and neural models. Section 2 describes the implementation. Section 3 uses the sensitivities from KPPax to analyse the identifiability of the rate coefficients of a benchmark mechanism before estimating them from noisy synthetic observations. Section 4 trains a neural-network correction of an emission inventory and shows that online fine-tuning through the chemical model improves on the offline two-step approach. Section 5 discusses the limitations, and Sect. 6 concludes. 2 Implementation of differentiable kinetic pre-processing 2.1 The chemistry kinetic problem An atmospheric chemical reaction system can be mathematically formulated by a coupled system of stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are numerically stiff, because reactive radical species relax on timescales of milliseconds to seconds, while longer-lived species evolve over hours, so the system’s Jacobian eigenvalues span many orders of magnitude. Explicit integration schemes are constrained by this stiffness to prohibitively small time steps for stability, rather than accuracy, and are therefore unsuitable, which is why KPP itself provides implicit and Rosenbrock-type solvers ( Sandu et al., 2003 ) . We integrate Eq. ( 4 ) using diffrax ( Kidger, 2022 ) , a JAX-native library of differentiable ODE solvers, selecting the implicit Kvaerno family of solvers, which combine embedded error estimates with an implicit treatment of the stiff terms via a diagonally implicit Runge-Kutta scheme, avoiding the step-size collapse of explicit methods. Step size is controlled adaptively by a proportional-integral (PID) controller, which adjusts d ​ t \mathrm{d}t to meet a prescribed local error tolerance rather than relying on a fixed or manually tuned step size. Because concentrations must remain strictly positive for the log-space rate law (Eq. 6 ), we additionally clip y y to a small positive floor at each evaluation of the right-hand side, preventing the solver from probing negative or exactly zero concentrations during error-controlled step adjustment. We perform all stiff ODE integration in 64-bit double precision. 2.3 Automatic differentiation Automatic differentiation (AD) computes exact derivatives of a numerical program by decomposing it into elementary operations and applying the chain rule systematically, either forward alongside the primal computation (forward mode) or backward from the output (reverse mode). Once the rate law and its numerical integration are expressed as JAX-traceable array operations, the sensitivity of an output quantity, for instance an observed concentration at time t F t_{F} , with respect to an input quantity, for instance an emission rate or a rate coefficient, can therefore be obtained automatically, without deriving the corresponding tangent-linear or adjoint equations by hand. Differentiating through an ODE solve is nonetheless a distinct problem from differentiating a single expression, since the numerical solution is produced by an iterative sequence of solver steps rather than a closed-form function. Two broad strategies exist for obtaining the required sensitivities, namely the optimize-then-discretize adjoint, which derives an adjoint ODE from the continuous forward equations and integrates it backwards independently of how the forward solve was discretised, and the discretize-then-optimize adjoint, which differentiates the forward numerical scheme itself, step by step, yielding the exact gradient of the numerical solution rather than an approximation to the gradient of the underlying continuous problem ( Sandu et al., 2003 ) . KPP implements both, but its discretize-then-optimize adjoint must be derived analytically for each integrator in turn. For example, Sandu et al. (2003) derive it explicitly for the linearly implicit Euler method, requiring not only the Jacobian but also its derivative with respect to concentration (the Hessian tensor) and dedicated sparse linear-algebra routines to evaluate it efficiently. They note this construction to be considerably more demanding than their optimize-then-discretize adjoint, and correspondingly, KPP provides hand-derived discretize-then-optimize adjoints for only a subset of its integrators. diffrax ( Kidger, 2022 ) instead obtains a discretize-then-optimize adjoint of the forward solve through reverse-mode AD applied directly to the solver’s internal steps, exposing the differentiation strategy as a configurable component of the solve rather than a property fixed by the choice of integrator. Naively differentiating through every accepted step this way would require storing each intermediate solver state, incurring memory cost proportional to the number of steps. The recursive checkpoint adjoint avoids this by checkpointing only a logarithmic subset of states and recomputing the remainder on demand during the backward pass, keeping memory cost sub-linear in step count while still returning the exact discrete gradient. Because this adjoint is generated automatically for any solver JAX can trace, KPPax removes the need to derive a Hessian or a solver-specific adjoint step by hand for every integrator, and with it the correctness risk that Sandu et al. (2003) themselves highlight for hand-written or general-purpose adjoint-compiler code. The trade-off is computational rather than conceptual: checkpointed recomputation adds cost that a hand-derived discretize-then-optimize adjoint, once implemented, would not incur, particularly for very large mechanisms. We consider this an acceptable exchange for the substantial reduction in implementation and maintenance effort it affords when extending KPPax to new mechanisms or integrators. 3 Application I: identifiability and parameter estimation Rate coefficients of atmospheric chem

items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.37631 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models Authors: Chang Su , Bin Wu , Emine Yilmaz , Yao Lu View a PDF of the paper titled What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models, by Chang Su and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores. Comments: Accepted to AACL 2026. items.content: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models Chang Su Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Email: sucha@engineering.upenn.edu Bin Wu Affiliation: Centre for Artificial Intelligence, University College London Email: bin.wu.23@ucl.ac.uk Emine Yilmaz Affiliation: Centre for Artificial Intelligence, University College London Email: emine.yilmaz@ucl.ac.uk Yao Lu Affiliation: Centre for Artificial Intelligence, University College London Email: yao.lu@cs.ucl.ac.uk Abstract Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item’s negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model–benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores. 1 Introduction Language models improve on a wide range of tasks as pretraining progresses, yet these gains reveal little about the characteristics of the knowledge being learned ( Swayamdipta et al., 2020 ; Chang et al., 2024 ) . We ask how different kinds of knowledge are learned at different stages of pretraining, using their prevalence in training data as a starting point for characterizing these differences. However, measuring how often a fact or concept appears in pretraining data is difficult because the same knowledge can be expressed in many different ways. Corpus search tools such as infini-gram ( Xu et al., 2025 ) count exact textual matches, but these counts depend on the wording of the query. Passages that express the same knowledge in different words may go uncounted, making exact-match frequency an incomplete measure of prevalence. The temporal structure of web corpora offers a complementary approach. Pretraining data combine web crawls collected in different years. Our intuition is that knowledge that appears consistently across these years should receive similar likelihoods from models trained on each yearly snapshot, even when its wording differs. Knowledge whose prevalence varies across years may instead receive more variable likelihoods. Point-in-time (PIT) language models, which share an architecture and training recipe but are trained on distinct yearly web snapshots ( Drinkall et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Kelly et al., 2026 ) , allow us to probe this variation. We propose a temporal variability score ( TVS \mathrm{TVS} ), defined as the coefficient of variation of the negative log-likelihood assigned to an item’s question and correct answer across eight yearly PIT-4B models ( Kelly et al., 2026 ) . Higher scores suggest that the underlying knowledge appears less consistently across years of web text. TVS \mathrm{TVS} measures likelihood variation, not prevalence directly. TVS \mathrm{TVS} enables a fine-grained analysis of knowledge acquisition during pretraining. We use individual items from widely used benchmarks spanning factual knowledge, scientific reasoning, and commonsense reasoning to assess what models learn at different stages. We compute TVS \mathrm{TVS} for 16,239 items from six multiple-choice benchmarks, divide each benchmark into length-matched low-, medium-, and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} groups, and track their accuracy across checkpoints of six models at different scales. We examine whether low- and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items exhibit different learning patterns at different stages of training. We find that low- and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items perform similarly early in training, but high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items improve faster at later stages. At the end of the pretraining runs, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items outperform low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items in 34 of 36 model–benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. The pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks: on ARC and MMLU, the advantage remains positive in all 18 settings when comparing items of similar difficulty. These findings connect temporal variability to differences in knowledge acquisition that aggregate benchmark scores can mask. Our contributions are as follows: • We propose TVS \mathrm{TVS} , an item-level diagnostic that uses point-in-time models to characterize sensitivity to training-data composition beyond exact textual matches. • We document differences in learning across TVS \mathrm{TVS} groups: items with higher temporal variability improve more at later training stages, with the most robust evidence on knowledge-intensive tasks. • We show that, on knowledge-intensive tasks, the component of TVS \mathrm{TVS} specific to the correct answer predicts growth in models’ preference for that answer during later training stages, among similarly difficult items. 2 Measuring Temporal Variability Point-in-time models. We use PIT-4B ( Kelly et al., 2026 ) , a suite of 4B-parameter base models trained on yearly partitions of FineWeb ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) . The eight models for 2017–2024 share architecture, tokenizer, and training setup and differ in the crawl year of their training data. Crawl years index when pages were collected, not when facts originated: each snapshot also contains older, long-lived content. Related PIT and time-stratified models are discussed in § 5 . Temporal variability score (TVS). We define the temporal variability score using the coefficient of variation (CV) across training snapshots: for item i i , let s i s_{i} be the string formed by the question and its gold answer, and let NLL y ​ ( s i ) \mathrm{NLL}_{y}(s_{i}) be the per-token negative log-likelihood of s i s_{i} under the PIT model for year y ∈ { 2017 , … , 2024 } y\in\{2017,\ldots,2024\} . We define TVS ⁡ ( i ) = std y ⁡ ( NLL y ​ ( s i ) ) mean y ⁡ ( NLL y ​ ( s i ) ) . \mathrm{TVS}(i)=\frac{\operatorname{std}_{y}(\mathrm{NLL}_{y}(s_{i}))}{\operatorname{mean}_{y}(\mathrm{NLL}_{y}(s_{i}))}. (1) Low TVS \mathrm{TVS} means that the yearly models agree on the item relative to its overall likelihood; we call such items temporally stable . High TVS \mathrm{TVS} means that the item’s likelihood depends on the training year; we call such items temporally variable . Normalizing by the mean matters. The coefficient of variation of perplexity is strongly entangled with mean perplexity; unnormalized NLL standard deviation mostly selects harder items (Appendix B ). Interpreting TVS. TVS \mathrm{TVS} measures relative cross-year variation in likelihood, not prevalence directly or semantic categories such as “commonsense” versus “specialized.” Each yearly model scores the same fixed question–answer string: time indexes the training snapshot, not a changing evaluation target. Stable and variable are likelihood-based labels; Table 1 illustrates groups, not a knowledge taxonomy. We also isolate correct-answer variation from the shared question and format (§ 4.3 ; Appendix D ). Benchmark TVS group Example (question → \rightarrow gold answer) PIQA Low “How do you take soap off of clean dishes?” → \rightarrow “rinse it in water.” PIQA High “To tell when baked goods are done baking, you can” → \rightarrow “Wait for them to turn golden brown.” ARC-Easy Low “What causes a change in the speed of a moving object?” → \rightarrow “Force.” ARC-Easy High “A meteoroid becomes a meteorite when it” → \rightarrow “impacts the surface of a planet.” Table 1: Sampled items from the low- and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} groups. 3 Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate on HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , WinoGrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2020 ) , ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , and MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . For each benchmark we sample 3,000 items from the training and validation splits (the test split for MMLU), or use all items when fewer are available, for 16,239 items in total. TVS \mathrm{TVS} is correlated with string length, so we stratify within length. We divide each benchmark into ten bins by PIT-4B token length, split each bin into equal low-, medium-, and high-TVS thirds, and pool the bins (Appendix B.2 ). Models. We evaluate checkpoints of six models from four open families 1 1 1 Checkpoints cover most of each training run, from 0.54B to 11.1T tokens; each trajectory is a single run. : Pythia 1.4B and 6.9B ( Biderman et al., 2023 ) , TinyLlama 1.1B ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , SmolLM3 3B ( Bakouch et al., 2025 ) , and OLMo 1B and 7B ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ) . 2 2 2 We use the 0724 versions of both OLMo models. Evaluation metric. Each item is scored by ranking its answer options by length-normalized likelihood. We report chance-normalized accuracy: acc norm = acc raw − chance 1 − chance . \operatorname{acc}_{\text{norm}}=\frac{\operatorname{acc}_{\text{raw}}-\operatorname{chance}}{1-\operatorname{chance}}. (2) This maps random guessing to 0 and perfect accuracy to 1 and makes benchmarks with different numbers of options comparable ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Kelly et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: Chance-normalized accuracy over pretraining for temporally variable (high TVS \mathrm{TVS} , red) and temporally stable (low TVS \mathrm{TVS} , green) items, by model (columns) and benchmark (rows). Groups are length-matched; training tokens are on a log scale. Pythia and OLMo show little early separation; high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items generally pull ahead later. 4 Results 4.1 Learning Patterns Diverge Across TVS Groups We examine how learning patterns differ across low- and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items as training progresses (Figure 1 ). Our earliest Pythia and OLMo checkpoints occur after 0.54B and 2B training tokens, respectively. At these checkpoints, low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items outperform high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items in 13 of 24 settings, no more often than expected by chance. The mean high-minus-low gap is − 0.8 -0.8 points of chance-normalized accuracy. The groups separate later: over the second half of the checkpoints, accuracy on high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items grows faster by 2.0 points per tenfold increase in training tokens. The difference is positive in 26 of 36 settings and in all six benchmark and model averages, but not significant across four family averages ( p = .13 p=.13 ; Appendix A.1 ). At the end of the pretraining runs, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items outperform low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items in 34 of 36 model–benchmark settings (Table 2 ). The mean gap is 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy (95% CI [5.5, 9.2]). It remains significant when settings are first averaged within each of the four model families (CI [4.8, 10.2], p = .003 p=.003 ), and it is positive on every benchmark, ranging from 1.7 points on WinoGrande to 16.1 points on PIQA (Appendix A.1 ). These intervals summarize variation across settings or family averages, not run-to-run uncertainty: each setting contains one training run. The pattern holds across model families trained on different corpora, which suggests that it is not tied to a single training recipe. Early Final Benchmarks L > > H H > > L Gap Gap ∣ \mid NLL All 13/24 34/36 +7.3 +3.7 HS/PIQA/WG 8/12 16/18 +8.5 +0.5 ARC/MMLU 5/12 18/18 +6.2 +6.9 Table 2: Low- (L) versus high-TVS (H) items at the earliest and final checkpoints. Early counts cover Pythia and OLMo, whose first checkpoints come early in training; final counts cover all six models. Gaps are high-minus-low chance-normalized accuracy in points. Gap ∣ \mid NLL uses a split conditioned on mean NLL (§ 4.2 ). 4.2 Does TVS Capture More Than Question Difficulty? To distinguish the relationship between TVS \mathrm{TVS} and learning from differences in question difficulty, we repeat the analysis using the variation in TVS \mathrm{TVS} not explained by mean NLL. We regress TVS \mathrm{TVS} on linear and quadratic mean-NLL terms within each benchmark and length bin, then divide the residuals into thirds. Within each length bin, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items have slightly lower mean NLL, making this adjustment relevant to the comparison. On ARC and MMLU, the advantage remains positive in all 18 settings, at +6.9 points of chance-normalized accuracy (Table 2 ). On HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande, the smaller gap (+0.5 points) indicates a substantial difficulty contribution (Appendix B.1 ). Conditioning additionally on PIT-4B’s gold-versus-distractor margin and accuracy leaves a final gap of 1.4 points, positive in 22 of 36 settings (Table 3 ). These covariates capture average likelihood and answer discrimination in the diagnostic suite; they need not exhaust difficulty for every evaluated model. The raw 7.3-point gap is not an estimate of an independent TVS \mathrm{TVS} effect; the remaining association varies across benchmarks. We also examine how the results depend on the measure used to group the same items (Table 3 ). Splitting directly by mean NLL produces the opposite ordering: the higher-NLL group performs worse in all 36 final settings. Replacing TVS \mathrm{TVS} with the unnormalized standard deviation of NLL also reverses the effect. This measure increases with mean NLL and therefore selects harder items. These comparisons distinguish the TVS \mathrm{TVS} pattern from those obtained by grouping items by mean NLL or unnormalized dispersion. Split (within length bins) Final H > > L Gap TVS \mathrm{TVS} (main) 34/36 +7.3 TVS \mathrm{TVS} ∣ \mid mean NLL 26/36 +3.7 TVS \mathrm{TVS} ∣ \mid mean NLL, PIT margin, PIT acc. 22/36 +1.4 Gold-vs.-wrong TVS \mathrm{TVS} margin 36/36 +12.3 Question-only TVS \mathrm{TVS} 26/36 +2.1 NLL standard deviation 8/36 − - 2.6 Mean NLL quintiles (high = harder) 0/36 − - 31.1 Table 3: Final-checkpoint comparison of high- versus low-group items under alternative stratifications (chance-normalized points; 36 model–benchmark settings). Conditioned splits use the residual of TVS \mathrm{TVS} after regressing out the listed covariates within each benchmark and length bin. Full results are in Table 5 . 4.3 Answer-Specific TVS Predicts Learning in Later Training Stages Answer options share a question and format, so we isolate correct-answer variation as its TVS \mathrm{TVS} minus the mean TVS \mathrm{TVS} of incorrect answers. We test whether it predicts growth in the correct-answer-versus-best-distractor margin, measured as its slope against log training tokens over the upper half of the log-token range. Margin growth need not change the top-ranked option, so we analyze it separately from final accuracy. Regressions include shared and answer-specific components, controlling for PIT-4B mean NLL, margin, and accuracy. The answer-specific signal predicts greater late margin growth on ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, and MMLU ( p < 10 − 6 p<10^{-6} each; Table 4 ), with a weaker effect on PIQA. On HellaSwag and WinoGrande, it predicts a small final-accuracy difference but no robust late-margin growth (Appendix D ). Group comparisons agree: the correct-answer-versus-strongest-distractor TVS \mathrm{TVS} margin yields the largest final gap, with the high group ahead in all 36 settings by 12.3 points on average and the best final group in 35. In contrast, question-only TVS \mathrm{TVS} yields an average gap of just 2.1 points (Appendices C.2 and C.1 ). Thus the relationship depends substantially on the answer itself, rather than only on question wording. Benchmark Final correct Late margin slope ARC-C +0.024 (.04) +0.070 ( 2 × 10 − 9 2\times 10^{-9} ) ARC-E +0.008 (.2) +0.059 ( 2 × 10 − 8 2\times 10^{-8} ) MMLU +0.001 (.8) +0.043 ( 2 × 10 − 7 2\times 10^{-7} ) PIQA +0.001 (.8) +0.011 ( 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} ) HellaSwag +0.019 ( 10 − 5 10^{-5} ) 0.000 (.8) WinoGrande +0.012 (.01) +0.002 (.08) Table 4: Difficulty-controlled effect of gold-specific TVS \mathrm{TVS} (per standard deviation) on final correctness and late gold-versus-distractor margin growth ( p p -values in parentheses; Appendix D ). 4.4 Assessing TVS Robustness to Benchmark Contamination We test for benchmark exposure in PIT-4B using release dates and textual overlap (Appendix F ). Benchmark copies should raise gold-answer likelihood after release. Yet staggered difference-in-differences with item and year fixed effects finds no decrease in gold-answer NLL ( + 0.016 +0.016 ) or detectable change in the gold-versus-distractor margin ( p = .34 p=.34 ). High- TVS \mathrm{TVS} accuracy falls slightly ( − 0.011 -0.011 , p = .004 p=.004 ), opposite the expected leakage effect. ARC, PIQA, and MMLU share similar year profiles despite different release dates, with no release-specific gains. We also scan 55B FineWeb tokens, using ten files per crawl year, for 13-gram overlap with each item ( Brown et al., 2020 ) . Overlap is rare (3.1% of high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} versus 2.0% of low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items) and mostly comes from source pages such as WikiHow rather than answer keys. Years with more overlap do not have lower PIT-4B NLL for the matched items. Adding overlap indicators to the item-level regressions leaves the TVS \mathrm{TVS} coefficient essentially unchanged. These checks provide evidence against benchmark leakage as the dominant explanation of the TVS \mathrm{TVS} pattern in PIT-4B, but sparse yearly sampling cannot establish its absence or exclude contamination of the evaluated models’ corpora. 5 Related Work Benchmark analysis. Dataset cartography characterizes items through a fine-tuned model’s training dynamics ( Swayamdipta et al., 2020 ) , while item response theory estimates their difficulty and discrimination ( Lalor et al., 2016 ; Martínez-Plumed et al., 2019 ) . Other approaches group benchmark items by difficulty or composition ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Kovatchev and Lease, 2024 ) . These measures describe items through the behavior of the evaluated models and can therefore vary with the model being diagnosed. TVS \mathrm{TVS} instead uses an external suite that shares architecture and training setup but differs in its temporal data slice. It therefore characterizes items independently of the evaluated model’s own training trajectory and supports comparisons across model families. Attributing learning to pretraining data. Models learn facts through repeated exposure ( Chang et al., 2024 ) , memorize more over training ( Tirumala et al., 2022 ) , and struggle with rare knowledge ( Kandpal et al., 2023 ) . Corpus search counts exact matches ( Elazar et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , making exposure estimates wording-dependent. Controlled ablations link capabilities to corpus components: removing parallel bilingual documents impairs translation but largely preserves cross-lingual question answering and reasoning ( Shao et al., 2026 ) . TVS \mathrm{TVS} complements these approaches by measuring sensitivity beyond exact overlap without requiring corpus interventions. Point-in-time language models. Time-stratified models probe temporal generalization and time-sensitive facts ( Lazaridou et al., 2021 ; Dhingra et al., 2022 ) ; PIT suites also address lookahead bias and historically bounded knowledge ( Drinkall et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Kelly et al., 2026 ) . We instead characterize fixed benchmark items through yearly likelihood variation, defining groups independently of evaluated checkpoints and comparing trajectories without their training corpora. Time indexes the corpus, not an intervention or changing targets. 6 Conclusion We introduced TVS \mathrm{TVS} to track item-level learning using point-in-time models. Across six benchmarks and six models, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items generally improve more later; the earliest Pythia and OLMo checkpoints show little group separation. Effects are most robust on ARC and MMLU, where difficulty-controlled, answer-specific TVS \mathrm{TVS} predicts late margin growth. TVS \mathrm{TVS} reveals dynamics beyond aggregate scores without requiring training-corpus access or assigning semantic categories to items. Limitations TVS \mathrm{TVS} is a model-based likelihood statistic, and its effectiveness therefore depends on the quality of the underlying model(s). The PIT-4B models cover crawl years 2017–2024 at a single model size. Our contamination checks cover the PIT-4B training data rather than the full pretraining corpora of the evaluated models (Appendix F ). Finally, we study only likelihood-ranked multiple-choice benchmarks as they are most suitable when monitoring models’ early checkpoints. (1) Low TVS \mathrm{TVS} means that the yearly models agree on the item relative to its overall likelihood; we call such items temporally stable . High TVS \mathrm{TVS} means that the item’s likelihood depends on the training year; we call such items temporally variable . Normalizing by the mean matters. The coefficient of variation of perplexity is strongly entangled with mean perplexity; unnormalized NLL standard deviation mostly selects harder items (Appendix B ). Interpreting TVS. TVS \mathrm{TVS} measures relative cross-year variation in likelihood, not prevalence directly or semantic categories such as “commonsense” versus “specialized.” Each yearly model scores the same fixed question–answer string: time indexes the training snapshot, not a changing evaluation target. Stable and variable are likelihood-based labels; Table 1 illustrates groups, not a knowledge taxonomy. We also isolate correct-answer variation from the shared question and format (§ 4.3 ; Appendix D ). Benchmark TVS group Example (question → \rightarrow gold answer) PIQA Low “How do you take soap off of clean dishes?” → \rightarrow “rinse it in water.” PIQA High “To tell when baked goods are done baking, you can” → \rightarrow “Wait for them to turn golden brown.” ARC-Easy Low “What causes a change in the speed of a moving object?” → \rightarrow “Force.” ARC-Easy High “A meteoroid becomes a meteorite when it” → \rightarrow “impacts the surface of a planet.” Table 1: Sampled items from the low- and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} groups. 3 Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate on HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , WinoGrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2020 ) , ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , and MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . For each benchmark we sample 3,000 items from the training and validation splits (the test split for MMLU), or use all items when fewer are available, for 16,239 items in total. TVS \mathrm{TVS} is correlated with string length, so we stratify within length. We divide each benchmark into ten bins by PIT-4B token length, split each bin into equal low-, medium-, and high-TVS thirds, and pool the bins (Appendix B.2 ). Models. We evaluate checkpoints of six models from four open families 1 1 1 Checkpoints cover most of each training run, from 0.54B to 11.1T tokens; each trajectory is a single run. : Pythia 1.4B and 6.9B ( Biderman et al., 2023 ) , TinyLlama 1.1B ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , SmolLM3 3B ( Bakouch et al., 2025 ) , and OLMo 1B and 7B ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ) . 2 2 2 We use the 0724 versions of both OLMo models. Evaluation metric. Each item is scored by ranking its answer options by length-normalized likelihood. We report chance-normalized accuracy: acc norm = acc raw − chance 1 − chance . \operatorname{acc}_{\text{norm}}=\frac{\operatorname{acc}_{\text{raw}}-\operatorname{chance}}{1-\operatorname{chance}}. (2) This maps random guessing to 0 and perfect accuracy to 1 and makes benchmarks with different numbers of options comparable ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Kelly et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: Chance-normalized accuracy over pretraining for temporally variable (high TVS \mathrm{TVS} , red) and temporally stable (low TVS \mathrm{TVS} , green) items, by model (columns) and benchmark (rows). Groups are length-matched; training tokens are on a log scale. Pythia and OLMo show little early separation; high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items generally pull ahead later. 4 Results 4.1 Learning Patterns Diverge Across TVS Groups We examine how learning patterns differ across low- and high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items as training progresses (Figure 1 ). Our earliest Pythia and OLMo checkpoints occur after 0.54B and 2B training tokens, respectively. At these checkpoints, low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items outperform high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items in 13 of 24 settings, no more often than expected by chance. The mean high-minus-low gap is − 0.8 -0.8 points of chance-normalized accuracy. The groups separate later: over the second half of the checkpoints, accuracy on high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items grows faster by 2.0 points per tenfold increase in training tokens. The difference is positive in 26 of 36 settings and in all six benchmark and model averages, but not significant across four family averages ( p = .13 p=.13 ; Appendix A.1 ). At the end of the pretraining runs, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items outperform low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items in 34 of 36 model–benchmark settings (Table 2 ). The mean gap is 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy (95% CI [5.5, 9.2]). It remains significant when settings are first averaged within each of the four model families (CI [4.8, 10.2], p = .003 p=.003 ), and it is positive on every benchmark, ranging from 1.7 points on WinoGrande to 16.1 points on PIQA (Appendix A.1 ). These intervals summarize variation across settings or family averages, not run-to-run uncertainty: each setting contains one training run. The pattern holds across model families trained on different corpora, which suggests that it is not tied to a single training recipe. Early Final Benchmarks L > > H H > > L Gap Gap ∣ \mid NLL All 13/24 34/36 +7.3 +3.7 HS/PIQA/WG 8/12 16/18 +8.5 +0.5 ARC/MMLU 5/12 18/18 +6.2 +6.9 Table 2: Low- (L) versus high-TVS (H) items at the earliest and final checkpoints. Early counts cover Pythia and OLMo, whose first checkpoints come early in training; final counts cover all six models. Gaps are high-minus-low chance-normalized accuracy in points. Gap ∣ \mid NLL uses a split conditioned on mean NLL (§ 4.2 ). 4.2 Does TVS Capture More Than Question Difficulty? To distinguish the relationship between TVS \mathrm{TVS} and learning from differences in question difficulty, we repeat the analysis using the variation in TVS \mathrm{TVS} not explained by mean NLL. We regress TVS \mathrm{TVS} on linear and quadratic mean-NLL terms within each benchmark and length bin, then divide the residuals into thirds. Within each length bin, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items have slightly lower mean NLL, making this adjustment relevant to the comparison. On ARC and MMLU, the advantage remains positive in all 18 settings, at +6.9 points of chance-normalized accuracy (Table 2 ). On HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande, the smaller gap (+0.5 points) indicates a substantial difficulty contribution (Appendix B.1 ). Conditioning additionally on PIT-4B’s gold-versus-distractor margin and accuracy leaves a final gap of 1.4 points, positive in 22 of 36 settings (Table 3 ). These covariates capture average likelihood and answer discrimination in the diagnostic suite; they need not exhaust difficulty for every evaluated model. The raw 7.3-point gap is not an estimate of an independent TVS \mathrm{TVS} effect; the remaining association varies across benchmarks. We also examine how the results depend on the measure used to group the same items (Table 3 ). Splitting directly by mean NLL produces the opposite ordering: the higher-NLL group performs worse in all 36 final settings. Replacing TVS \mathrm{TVS} with the unnormalized standard deviation of NLL also reverses the effect. This measure increases with mean NLL and therefore selects harder items. These comparisons distinguish the TVS \mathrm{TVS} pattern from those obtained by grouping items by mean NLL or unnormalized dispersion. Split (within length bins) Final H > > L Gap TVS \mathrm{TVS} (main) 34/36 +7.3 TVS \mathrm{TVS} ∣ \mid mean NLL 26/36 +3.7 TVS \mathrm{TVS} ∣ \mid mean NLL, PIT margin, PIT acc. 22/36 +1.4 Gold-vs.-wrong TVS \mathrm{TVS} margin 36/36 +12.3 Question-only TVS \mathrm{TVS} 26/36 +2.1 NLL standard deviation 8/36 − - 2.6 Mean NLL quintiles (high = harder) 0/36 − - 31.1 Table 3: Final-checkpoint comparison of high- versus low-group items under alternative stratifications (chance-normalized points; 36 model–benchmark settings). Conditioned splits use the residual of TVS \mathrm{TVS} after regressing out the listed covariates within each benchmark and length bin. Full results are in Table 5 . 4.3 Answer-Specific TVS Predicts Learning in Later Training Stages Answer options share a question and format, so we isolate correct-answer variation as its TVS \mathrm{TVS} minus the mean TVS \mathrm{TVS} of incorrect answers. We test whether it predicts growth in the correct-answer-versus-best-distractor margin, measured as its slope against log training tokens over the upper half of the log-token range. Margin growth need not change the top-ranked option, so we analyze it separately from final accuracy. Regressions include shared and answer-specific components, controlling for PIT-4B mean NLL, margin, and accuracy. The answer-specific signal predicts greater late margin growth on ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, and MMLU ( p < 10 − 6 p<10^{-6} each; Table 4 ), with a weaker effect on PIQA. On HellaSwag and WinoGrande, it predicts a small final-accuracy difference but no robust late-margin growth (Appendix D ). Group comparisons agree: the correct-answer-versus-strongest-distractor TVS \mathrm{TVS} margin yields the largest final gap, with the high group ahead in all 36 settings by 12.3 points on average and the best final group in 35. In contrast, question-only TVS \mathrm{TVS} yields an average gap of just 2.1 points (Appendices C.2 and C.1 ). Thus the relationship depends substantially on the answer itself, rather than only on question wording. Benchmark copies should raise gold-answer likelihood after release. Yet staggered difference-in-differences with item and year fixed effects finds no decrease in gold-answer NLL ( + 0.016 +0.016 ) or detectable change in the gold-versus-distractor margin ( p = .34 p=.34 ). High- TVS \mathrm{TVS} accuracy falls slightly ( − 0.011 -0.011 , p = .004 p=.004 ), opposite the expected leakage effect. ARC, PIQA, and MMLU share similar year profiles despite different release dates, with no release-specific gains. We also scan 55B FineWeb tokens, using ten files per crawl year, for 13-gram overlap with each item ( Brown et al., 2020 ) . Overlap is rare (3.1% of high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} versus 2.0% of low- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items) and mostly comes from source pages such as WikiHow rather than answer keys. Years with more overlap do not have lower PIT-4B NLL for the matched items. Adding overlap indicators to the item-level regressions leaves the TVS \mathrm{TVS} coefficient essentially unchanged. These checks provide evidence against benchmark leakage as the dominant explanation of the TVS \mathrm{TVS} pattern in PIT-4B, but sparse yearly sampling cannot establish its absence or exclude contamination of the evaluated models’ corpora. 5 Related Work Benchmark analysis. Dataset cartography characterizes items through a fine-tuned model’s training dynamics ( Swayamdipta et al., 2020 ) , while item response theory estimates their difficulty and discrimination ( Lalor et al., 2016 ; Martínez-Plumed et al., 2019 ) . Other approaches group benchmark items by difficulty or composition ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Kovatchev and Lease, 2024 ) . These measures describe items through the behavior of the evaluated models and can therefore vary with the model being diagnosed. TVS \mathrm{TVS} instead uses an external suite that shares architecture and training setup but differs in its temporal data slice. It therefore characterizes items independently of the evaluated model’s own training trajectory and supports comparisons across model families. Attributing learning to pretraining data. Models learn facts through repeated exposure ( Chang et al., 2024 ) , memorize more over training ( Tirumala et al., 2022 ) , and struggle with rare knowledge ( Kandpal et al., 2023 ) . Corpus search counts exact matches ( Elazar et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , making exposure estimates wording-dependent. Controlled ablations link capabilities to corpus components: removing parallel bilingual documents impairs translation but largely preserves cross-lingual question answering and reasoning ( Shao et al., 2026 ) . TVS \mathrm{TVS} complements these approaches by measuring sensitivity beyond exact overlap without requiring corpus interventions. Point-in-time language models. Time-stratified models probe temporal generalization and time-sensitive facts ( Lazaridou et al., 2021 ; Dhingra et al., 2022 ) ; PIT suites also address lookahead bias and historically bounded knowledge ( Drinkall et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Kelly et al., 2026 ) . We instead characterize fixed benchmark items through yearly likelihood variation, defining groups independently of evaluated checkpoints and comparing trajectories without their training corpora. Time indexes the corpus, not an intervention or changing targets. 6 Conclusion We introduced TVS \mathrm{TVS} to track item-level learning using point-in-time models. Across six benchmarks and six models, high- TVS \mathrm{TVS} items generally improve more later; the earliest Pythia and OLMo checkpoints show little group separation. Effects are most robust on ARC and MMLU, where difficulty-controlled, answer-specific TVS \mathrm{TVS} predicts late margin growth. TVS \mathrm{TVS} reveals dynamics beyond aggregate scores without requiring training-corpus access or assigning semantic categories to items. Limitations TVS \mathrm{TVS} is a model-based likelihood statistic, and its effectiveness therefore depends on the quality of the underlying model(s). The PIT-4B models cover crawl years 2017–2024 at a single model size. Our contamination checks cover the PIT-4B training data rather than the full pretraining corpora of the evaluated models (Appendix F ). Finally, we study only likelihood-ranked multiple-choice benchmarks as they are most suitable when monitoring models’ early checkpoints. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.37624 (cs) [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026] Title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions Authors: Anouar Imel , Imad Charradi , Abderrahman Sghir , Khalil El Khammar View a PDF of the paper titled Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions, by Anouar Imel and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all. Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. Memory architectures maintain information across interactions ( Packer et al. 2023 ; Park et al. 2023 ) , and prompt compression and selective context address limited capacity ( Jiang et al. 2023 ; Li et al. 2023 ) . Benchmarks of conversational memory test long-horizon recall ( Maharana et al. 2024 ) , and recent multi-party benchmarks show that memory pipelines lose speaker and group structure ( Yang et al. 2026 ; Hu et al. 2026 ) ; CrossProfile instead asks which evidence a compressed memory should keep for a downstream decision. Interaction-aware selection argues that records can matter only in combination ( Subrahmanyam and Choudhary 2026 ) , which is consistent with our finding that decisions follow the balance of the kept evidence rather than the merit of individual facts. Position effects further separate available evidence from evidence the model uses ( Liu et al. 2024 ) ; our tag controls hold line order fixed to separate attribution from position. 3 Setting and Memory Policies Figure 2: Pipeline. Facts from template M01 (Table 4 ) are distributed among the agents; HiddenBench tasks have three or four agents and CrossProfile tasks have four. After the discussion, a memory policy compresses it under a token budget B B , either by summarizing the transcript (B3) or by selecting whole claims from a claim inventory (R1, R1-rel, B4, Random). A separate call with the same model weights answers from the task and the memory alone. 3.1 Discussion, Memory, and Decision A task specifies a description, candidate answers, and facts assigned to agents. A shared fact is held by every agent; a private fact is held by one. After the discussion, a memory policy constructs a memory for a separate decision call, which receives only the description, the options, and the memory. The decision call uses the same model weights as the discussion and sees the full transcript only in the REF control. Answer keys and role labels are withheld from all generation and from every memory policy except the oracle-relevance control. In controlled HiddenBench discussions, each agent is scripted to state its assigned facts. Natural discussions consist of initial individual votes, two rounds of messages, and final votes; memories are built from the messages, not the votes. Copy policies select from a known claim inventory in the controlled condition and from an extracted inventory in the natural condition. In extracted inventories, a claim’s contributors are the agents who stated it, which need not coincide with the agents who originally held the underlying fact. The summary policy B3 reads the transcript directly. Figure 2 summarizes these paths. 3.2 The CrossProfile Benchmark CrossProfile has 60 main templates, five in each of 12 decision domains. Each template has four agents, three options, and 12 facts: five support, three decoy, and four irrelevant. Support facts favor the correct option, including negative evidence about the decoy option. Decoy facts favor the competing option, including negative evidence about the correct option. Both concern the stated decision criteria; decoys are true statements whose partial implication is misleading. Irrelevant facts concern other attributes and may be positive or negative in tone. Each role group is independently shared or private, yielding 2 3 2^{3} ownership variants and 480 derived tasks. Ten pilot templates are excluded from all main estimates. The answer key follows from the structured facts: each favorable fact adds one to its option’s score, each unfavorable fact subtracts one, and irrelevant facts contribute zero. An automatic verifier checks every template for a unique best option over all facts, a decoy win when only decoy facts are counted, a correct-option win when only support facts are counted, and the absence of hint words; all 70 templates pass. With the fixed fact counts, the keyed option scores + 2 +2 over all facts and each competitor scores 0 0 . The task description asks for the best overall record on equally weighted criteria, but the decision prompt does not state the scoring rule. Accuracy therefore measures agreement with this constructed key. The controlled transcript randomizes the speaking order and the order of each speaker’s facts. Every shared fact appears in the first speaker’s turn, although not necessarily before every private fact in that turn, so first-mention selection is sensitive to prevalence. Copied memory lines keep their contributor tags and follow the policy’s selection order. Ownership thus changes how evidence is presented as well as its selection priority. 3.3 Memory Policies and Budgets R1 orders claims by increasing contributor count, breaking ties by first appearance. B4 orders claims by first appearance alone. Random orders the same inventory uniformly at random. These copy policies add whole claims in this order until the budget is reached, skipping any claim that would exceed it. B3 , the evidence-preserving summary, asks the model to keep each distinct piece of evidence with its conditions, uncertainty, and disagreements. It receives a word limit derived from the budget, and longer outputs are truncated to the budget. R1-rel first asks the model which fact texts concern the stated criteria. This filter sees the description, options, and fact texts, but no holders, answers, or role labels. Claims predicted relevant form the first tier and the remaining claims the second, with R1 order inside each tier; second-tier claims remain eligible. Since decoys concern the criteria, they are relevant by this definition.
