items.content: Timestral Abstract We introduce Timestral , a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/timestral and inference code on GitHub 2 2 2 https://github.com/mistralai/timestral . Webpage: https://mistral.ai/news/timestral 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Forecast error against parameter count on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench (lower is better; fev-bench skill scores are shown as one minus the skill score). The dashed and solid curves show the Pareto fronts without and with Timestral, respectively. All four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front across the six panels. \Acp tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem ( Ansari et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2024 ) . Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates ( Khwaja et al., 2026 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Podest et al., 2026 ; Meyer et al., 2026 ) . These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use. Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0 ( Ansari et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two. Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass. To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively. cpm ( cpm ), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3 ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Khwaja et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sen, 2026 ) , achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence. The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking. Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden. We introduce Timestral , a family of four foundation models for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed time series forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. All four models share the same architecture and training recipe, offering a range of trade-offs between forecast accuracy and inference cost. Timestral addresses the coupling of horizons and context masking through dhf ( dhf ), which separates causal context representations from learned prediction tokens, and the covariate challenge through a role-aware covariate framework that integrates known-future information while preserving target causality. The models are pretrained on a synthetic corpus of univariate signals and structured multivariate dependencies, then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context. Timestral-209M sets a new state of the art in forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench. As shown in Figure 1 , all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front for all benchmark metrics. Timestral-123M already outperforms every other model shown, including models with billions of parameters. This report presents the released Timestral models, their benchmark results, and the main design choices behind them: • dhf . We introduce dhf , a forecasting formulation that separates missing observations from prediction tokens. dhf preserves observed values as context for later forecast origins within the same training sequence, allowing multiple forecast blocks to be supervised while controlling horizon sampling independently of artificial context masking. • Covariate conditioning within dhf . We integrate past-only and known-future covariates through explicit series roles and asymmetric attention. This enables prediction tokens to use known-future information at multiple forecast origins while preserving causality over target values. • A model family spanning accuracy and inference cost. We release four model sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters. The 209M model ranks first on all reported metrics among the models compared on GIFT-Eval ( Aksu et al., 2024 ) , TIME ( Qiao et al., 2026 ) , and fev-bench ( Shchur et al., 2026 ) . 2 Background We first describe tsfm within the framework of pfn , which interprets forecasting as amortised posterior inference ( Section 2.1 ). We then review how current tsfm model dependencies across variates and over time, and the drawbacks that motivate the design of Timestral ( Section 2.2 ). 2.1 Time Series Foundation Models as Prior-Data Fitted Networks Synthetic data has become a standard ingredient of tsfm training, and its share has generally grown. TimesFM mixes 20% synthetic series built from ARMA processes, seasonal patterns, trends, and steps ( Das et al., 2024 ) ; Chronos samples 10% of its training series from KernelSynth, a Gaussian-process generator ( Ansari et al., 2024 ) ; and TiRex draws about a third of its training series from an extended KernelSynth generator ( Auer et al., 2025 ) . More recent models rely on synthetic data more heavily: 57.5% of Toto-2.0’s pretraining mix is generated with TempoPFN’s generators ( Khwaja et al., 2026 ) , and Chronos-2 learns its multivariate and covariate capabilities from synthetic data only, with a variant trained without any real data performing only slightly worse than the full model ( Ansari et al., 2025 ) . At the other end, time series pfn such as ForecastPFN, Mamba4Cast, TimePFN, and TempoPFN are trained exclusively on synthetic data ( Dooley et al., 2023 ; Bhethanabhotla et al., 2024 ; Taga et al., 2025 ; Moroshan et al., 2026 ) . Timestral follows this direction: it is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, and a significant part of our effort went into designing the generating processes. The pfn framework provides a principled view of this choice, in which the generators define a prior over processes and forecasting becomes approximate Bayesian inference under that prior. Given the observed history 𝐲 1 : t \mathbf{y}_{1:t} of the target variates (the context), the task is to produce forecasts 𝐲 ^ t + 1 : t + H \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t+1:t+H} for the next H H time steps. From a Bayesian perspective, a probabilistic forecast should follow the ppd ( ppd ). If the series is generated by an unknown process f f drawn from a prior p ⁡ ( f ) p(f) , the ppd integrates over all processes consistent with the context, p ( 𝐲 t + 1 : t + H ∣ 𝐲 1 : t ) = ∫ p ( 𝐲 t + 1 : t + H ∣ 𝐲 1 : t , f ) p ( f ∣ 𝐲 1 : t ) d f . p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H}\mid\mathbf{y}_{1:t})=\int p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H}\mid\mathbf{y}_{1:t},f)\,p(f\mid\mathbf{y}_{1:t})\,\mathrm{d}f. (1) It accounts for both the noise of a given process and the uncertainty about which process generated the context. Covariates enter as further conditioning variables and are omitted for brevity. \Acp pfn ( Müller et al., 2022 ) learn to approximate the ppd during training: each training example draws a process f ∼ p ⁡ ( f ) f\sim p(f) and a dataset from f f , and the network predicts held-out values from the observed ones. In tabular pfn ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ; Hollmann et al., 2025 ) , f f can be a random scm that generates context rows of features and targets; the network then predicts the targets of further rows from their features. In time series pfn , f f generates a context 𝐲 1 : t \mathbf{y}_{1:t} (optionally with covariates) and the network predicts its continuation 𝐲 t + 1 : t + H \mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H} as in Equation 1 . When trained with the negative log-likelihood, the network’s optimal prediction is the ppd . The network thus amortises posterior inference over f f : instead of fitting a model to each new series, it infers from the context which processes are plausible and approximates the ppd in a single forward pass. \Acp tsfm differ from this setting in two respects but admit the same interpretation. First, many recent tsfm are trained with the pinball loss ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Khwaja et al., 2026 ) . With the pinball loss, the optimal prediction is not the full ppd but its quantiles ( Koenker and Bassett, 1978 ) : for each future time step and quantile level τ \tau , the network learns the τ \tau -quantile of the ppd at that time step. Second, their prior is not defined by synthetic generators alone: real series, viewed as draws from unknown processes, are also used, for example in continued training as in recent tabular pfn ( Garg et al., 2025 ) , so the full training data and its augmentations form the prior. In this view, a tsfm approximates the ppd under the prior defined by its training data. This prior determines which processes are plausible for a given context and thus how uncertain the forecasts are. A prior with too much unpredictable variability widens forecasts even for regular series, whereas one with too little makes the model overconfident. The composition of the training data is therefore a central design choice for tsfm . 2.2 Time Series Foundation Model Architectures Patch-based forecasting. Following PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2023 ) , most modern tsfm represent a time series as a sequence of non-overlapping patches ( Das et al., 2024 ; Woo et al., 2024 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Khwaja et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sen, 2026 ) . Each patch i i of P P consecutive time steps of a target variate is mapped to a token embedding 𝐯 i \mathbf{v}_{i} , reducing the token sequence length by a factor of P P . A sequence-modelling backbone, such as a Transformer, state-space model, or rnn , processes these context tokens and computes patch-based representations 𝐡 j \mathbf{h}_{j} for the forecast horizon. A prediction head maps these representations back to time-step resolution, producing forecasts for future patch j j . This is commonly a quantile head, which predicts conditional quantiles for each time step to represent forecast uncertainty ( Ansari et al., 2025 ; Khwaja et al., 2026 ) . Multivariate forecasting and covariates. Multivariate forecasting allows predictions for each target variate to depend on both its own history and the histories of other target variates. Covariates 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} provide additional inputs without themselves being forecast. Past-only covariates (patch embeddings 𝐜 i past \mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{past}}_{i} ) supply historical values, while known-future covariates (patch embeddings 𝐜 i fut \mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{fut}}_{i} ) supply both historical values and values known in advance over the forecast horizon. Toto-2.0 and Chronos-2 use cross-variate attention to exchange information between variates at the same patch position. Toto-2.0 replaces temporal attention in its final Transformer block with variate attention, whereas Chronos-2 applies both temporal and variate attention in every Transformer block ( Khwaja et al., 2026 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ) . Chronos-2 supports both covariate types within its group-attention formulation. Bidirectional temporal modelling. Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 ( Ansari et al., 2025 ) and Falcon-2.0 ( Xia et al., 2026 ) process the observed context together with tokens at future prediction positions, without exposing future values of the target variates. items.raw_text: Timestral Abstract We introduce Timestral , a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/timestral and inference code on GitHub 2 2 2 https://github.com/mistralai/timestral . Webpage: https://mistral.ai/news/timestral 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Forecast error against parameter count on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench (lower is better; fev-bench skill scores are shown as one minus the skill score). The dashed and solid curves show the Pareto fronts without and with Timestral, respectively. All four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front across the six panels. \Acp tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem ( Ansari et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2024 ) . Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates ( Khwaja et al., 2026 ; Ansari et al., 2025 ; Podest et al., 2026 ; Meyer et al., 2026 ) . These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use. Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0 ( Ansari et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two. Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass. To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively. cpm ( cpm ), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3 ( Auer et al., 2025 ; Khwaja et al., 2026 ; Jain and Sen, 2026 ) , achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence. The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking. Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden. We introduce Timestral , a family of four foundation models for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed time series forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. All four models share the same architecture and training recipe, offering a range of trade-offs between forecast accuracy and inference cost. Timestral addresses the coupling of horizons and context masking through dhf ( dhf ), which separates causal context representations from learned prediction tokens, and the covariate challenge through a role-aware covariate framework that integrates known-future information while preserving target causality. The models are pretrained on a synthetic corpus of univariate signals and structured multivariate dependencies, then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context. Timestral-209M sets a new state of the art in forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench. As shown in Figure 1 , all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front for all benchmark metrics. Timestral-123M already outperforms every other model shown, including models with billions of parameters. This report presents the released Timestral models, their benchmark results, and the main design choices behind them: • dhf . We introduce dhf , a forecasting formulation that separates missing observations from prediction tokens. dhf preserves observed values as context for later forecast origins within the same training sequence, allowing multiple forecast blocks to be supervised while controlling horizon sampling independently of artificial context masking. • Covariate conditioning within dhf . We integrate past-only and known-future covariates through explicit series roles and asymmetric attention. This enables prediction tokens to use known-future information at multiple forecast origins while preserving causality over target values. • A model family spanning accuracy and inference cost. We release four model sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters. The 209M model ranks first on all reported metrics among the models compared on GIFT-Eval ( Aksu et al., 2024 ) , TIME ( Qiao et al., 2026 ) , and fev-bench ( Shchur et al., 2026 ) . 2 Background We first describe tsfm within the framework of pfn , which interprets forecasting as amortised posterior inference ( Section 2.1 ). We then review how current tsfm model dependencies across variates and over time, and the drawbacks that motivate the design of Timestral ( Section 2.2 ). 2.1 Time Series Foundation Models as Prior-Data Fitted Networks Synthetic data has become a standard ingredient of tsfm training, and its share has generally grown. TimesFM mixes 20% synthetic series built from ARMA processes, seasonal patterns, trends, and steps ( Das et al., 2024 ) ; Chronos samples 10% of its training series from KernelSynth, a Gaussian-process generator ( Ansari et al., 2024 ) ; and TiRex draws about a third of its training series from an extended KernelSynth generator ( Auer et al., 2025 ) . More recent models rely on synthetic data more heavily: 57.5% of Toto-2.0’s pretraining mix is generated with TempoPFN’s generators ( Khwaja et al., 2026 ) , and Chronos-2 learns its multivariate and covariate capabilities from synthetic data only, with a variant trained without any real data performing only slightly worse than the full model ( Ansari et al., 2025 ) . At the other end, time series pfn such as ForecastPFN, Mamba4Cast, TimePFN, and TempoPFN are trained exclusively on synthetic data ( Dooley et al., 2023 ; Bhethanabhotla et al., 2024 ; Taga et al., 2025 ; Moroshan et al., 2026 ) . Timestral follows this direction: it is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, and a significant part of our effort went into designing the generating processes. The pfn framework provides a principled view of this choice, in which the generators define a prior over processes and forecasting becomes approximate Bayesian inference under that prior. These are copies of a single learned embedding, distinguished by their temporal position: 𝐩 j \mathbf{p}_{j} takes the same temporal position as the context token 𝐯 j \mathbf{v}_{j} . Both kinds of tokens are processed by the same Transformer, with shared parameters. Each 𝐩 j \mathbf{p}_{j} attends to the context tokens before its block and to the prediction tokens 𝐩 b , … , 𝐩 j \mathbf{p}_{b},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{j} of its own block, whereas context tokens never attend to prediction tokens. Context and prediction tokens thus form two separate streams. The resulting output 𝐡 j \mathbf{h}_{j} is passed to the prediction head to forecast patch j j and therefore depends only on 𝐯 0 , … , 𝐯 b − 1 \mathbf{v}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{b-1} and 𝐩 b , … , 𝐩 j \mathbf{p}_{b},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{j} . Outputs at context tokens are not passed to the prediction head and receive no direct loss. To train forecasts at many forecast distances, each training sequence is tiled into consecutive forecast blocks whose lengths are sampled from a block-length distribution. A block of length k k contains one forecast at each distance 1 , … , k 1,\ldots,k , so this distribution determines how often each forecast distance is trained. Because context tokens never attend to prediction tokens, the context representations are computed once and shared by all blocks of a training sequence. As in causal decoder-only models ( Figure 2(b) ), a single training sequence thus provides training signal from forecasts at many starting points, but in dhf , the forecast from each starting point can extend several patches ahead. Unlike cpm , dhf does not mask context patches to create longer forecast distances. In cpm , a forecast at distance d d requires masking the d − 1 d-1 patches before its target, and these patches are then also missing from the context of all later forecasts, so training longer forecast distances removes context. In dhf , each patch in a forecast block has two tokens during training: its prediction token, at which it is forecast, and its context token, which keeps its observed values available to later blocks. In Figure 5 , for instance, the forecasts of the third block depend on 𝐯 2 \mathbf{v}_{2} , which cpm masks. This decoupling has the following advantages. First, how often each forecast distance is trained can be tuned without side effects on the context. Second, missing data can be simulated independently of the forecast distances: optional missing-data augmentation hides variable-length gaps at arbitrary time steps rather than whole patches, which is closer to realistic missing-data distributions, and the hidden values are still scored as targets. Third, missing values, whether in the data or introduced by augmentation, are flagged in their context tokens and thus represented differently from forecast positions, whereas cpm represents a patch masked for forecasting in the same way as a fully missing patch. These advantages come at the cost of roughly doubling the number of tokens during training, since forecast blocks tile the full sequence so that every patch except the first serves as a forecast target. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback.
